title: Disney Earnings Buoyed By ‘Toy Story 5’, Theme Parks, Streaming Profit; Books $100M Tariff Refund
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith , Dade Hayes August 5, 2026 4:05am Toy Story 5 Disney Disney ’s Josh D’Amaro stepped out with solid numbers and some news in his first full quarter as CEO. Toy Story 5 drove studio revenue, theme parks saw an uptick in attendance, and streaming profits more than doubled for the three months ended in June. Total operating income for Disney’s fiscal third quarter jumped 21% $5.6 billion, beating Wall Street forecasts, as did adjusted EPS (of $2.06 a share, up from $1.61). Revenue of $25.2 billion rose 7% from the year earlier. The fiscal Q3 numbers follow confirmation of Disney’s planned sale of its 50% interest in A+E Global Media to an affiliate of co-owner Hearst for $1.2 billion in cash. The media giant is moving its consumer products business under Studios from the lucrative division’s longtime home in Experiences. And it unveiled a global, short form content sharing partnership with TikTok this morning. Related Stories News David Ellison Says Paramount Is "Absolutely Open" To Settling WBD Antitrust Suit, But "We Will Win At Trial" News Disney Closes $1.2 Billion Deal To Sell A+E Global Media Stake To Hearst The quarterly numbers and full-year outlook “reinforce our confidence that we are uniquely well positioned,” said D’Amaro, who took the reins from Bob Iger in March. “Decades of IP investment have built deep fan connections that translate into strong financial results. Our accelerating global guests growth at Experiences, Toy Story 5 ‘s theatrical and consumer products success, and strong ESPN viewership gains all helped expand our consumer reach this quarter.” Watch on Deadline He’ll be hosting a call with analysts at 8:30 am ET. Disney’s three sprawling divisions are led by Entertainment, which posted profit of $1.7 billion, up 64%, on revenue of $11.3 billion. The company cited the June 19 theatrical release of Toy Story 5 , which has surpassed $1 billion in global box office, as well as The Devil Wears Prada 2. Disney acknowledged that Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu and live action Moana (in fiscal 4Q) underperformed at the box office but noted their other contributions to the flywheel like a new Mandalorian-themed Millennium Falcon: Smuggler’s Run at Disneyland and Walt Disney World , and retail sales. “We expect the live-action Moana to be a strong title on Disney+ , building on the success of the original film … and extending the reach of the franchise, which now includes three films, a themed area at EPCOT, and a robust global merchandise business.” Disney doesn’t furnish streaming subscriber numbers anymore but said SVOD operating income more than doubled to $712 million from $329 million on revenue of $5.5 billion, up 11%. Subscriptions fees rose 15% (9% from more subscribers, 3% from higher rates and 1% from a favorable foreign exchange impact). Advertising nosed up 3% (impressions were higher, rates lower). Disney also sounded a bit like Netflix as it talked up an emerging international programming slate with Rivals Season 2 on Disney+ in the U.K. and Ireland, The Perfect Crown in Korea and Dear Killer Nannies in Latin America. The company plans to triple the number of Disney+ local original series over the next three years. “Our ambition is for Disney+ to become the digital centerpiece of the Walt Disney Company,” D’Amaro’s letter said. “We aim to evolve Disney+ into a comprehensive membership ecosystem. By integrating high-value, always-on benefits with our storytelling, we can reach more fans, deepen engagement, and increase subscriber retention. These product enhancements will also allow us to further segment the market, increasing our addressable opportunity over time. We expect to begin introducing elements of this vision in Spring 2027.” Disney+ Q3 churn declined worldwide and Disney said it passed an important milestone in “app unification” allowing Hulu standalone and bundle subscribers to link profiles, watch history, and manage subscriptions on Disney+. At Experiences, profit rose 20% to over $3 billion on almost $10 billion in revenue. Global guests grew 4% and attendance at domestic parks rose 3%. WDW saw healthy core attendance increases from domestic tourists and annual passholders.Forward bookings remain robust. That should reassure investors who were spooked by softer attendance at Universal’s domestic parks when Comcast reported earnings last month. Theme parks average per capita ticket revenue rose 5%. Disney noted continued, but moderating, headwinds from international attendance at domestic parks. It cited strong attendance growth at Disneyland Paris following the opening of World of Frozen. Overall, it anticipates a quarter of global guest growth in the current fiscal Q4 despite consumer softness in Asia. Q3 was the first full quarter with Disney’s two newest cruise ships, the Disney Destiny and Disney Adventure. Disney said it recorded approximately $100 million in a tariff refund for the quarter, reversing out tariff payments earlier in the fiscal year. Apple last week reported a $2.19 billion tariff refund for the June quarter. Sports, led by juggernaut ESPN, saw profit of $853 million, down 17% on higher programming and production costs, on $4.5 billion in revenue. Disney cited contractual rate increases, costs for new sports rights and an impact from the timing of rights costs recognition as a result of the NBA contract renewal. Contributing to the lower-than-expected operating income were four-game sweeps in early rounds of the NBA playoffs and the impact of a network carriage dispute. Disney was likely referring here to the resolution terms of a fight with YouTube TV in late 2025. After unlocking a selection of ESPN content on Disney+ domestically in 2024 and expanding it globally since then, the letter said, the company plans to deliver a more robust subset of games for Disney+ subscribers beginning this fall anchored by additional college football simulcasts. The service will also continue simulcasting college football pregame show College GameDay . title: Prateek Kuhad to Make Feature Film Acting Debut in Marginal MediaWorks, D36 and Jugaad’s ‘Drowning,’ Directed by Dar Gai (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 5, 2026 4:00am PT Prateek Kuhad to Make Feature Film Acting Debut in Marginal MediaWorks, D36 and Jugaad’s ‘Drowning,’ Directed by Dar Gai (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Cannibalism Comedy-Horror ‘Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,’ Starring Amir Nafis, Signs Abnormal Studios for Worldwide Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 10 hours ago Cate Blanchett, Nina Hoss on the Friendship Driving ‘Elektra/Persona’ at London’s National Theatre: ‘There’s a Lot of Masking and Unmasking’ 14 hours ago Tokyo’s TIFFCOM 2026 Expands IP Market, Adds AI and Anime Conferences 22 hours ago See All Marginal MediaWorks Prateek Kuhad , the Indian singer-songwriter known for hits including “Cold/Mess” and “Kasoor,” will make his feature film acting debut in “ Drowning ” (“Doobna” in Hindi/Urdu), Marginal MediaWorks has revealed. Directed by Dar Gai and shot on location in New Delhi, the film marks Marginal’s first fiction feature produced in South Asia, in partnership with Los Angeles-based label D36 and Mumbai-based Jugaad Motion Pictures. Related Stories Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Kuhad plays Tarush, an indie musician in Delhi who lands one breakout hit and then can’t escape the grip of a criminal record label boss. Marginal founder and CEO Sanjay M. Sharma is producing with the company’s head of film, Milan Chakraborty, D36 co-founder and CEO Abhi Kanakadandila, and Jugaad co-founders Dheer Momaya and Gai, from a story the group developed jointly. Popular on Variety “The film is like if the Safdie brothers mixed John Carney’s ‘Once’ and Lars von Trier’s ‘Dancer in the Dark’ in the blender that is the contemporary music scene in Delhi,” Sharma said. For Kuhad, the project grew out of an earlier collaboration with Gai, who directed the video for his song “Cold/Mess.” “Ever since Dar directed the video for ‘Cold/Mess’ I hoped we would find more ways to work together,” Kuhad said. “So when Abhi and Sanjay brought the idea for a film inspired by my song ‘Drown,’ I was immediately intrigued.” Kuhad’s “Cold/Mess” reached No. 1 on Spotify India and was featured on former U.S. President Barack Obama’s year-end playlist; the Gai-directed video was later named Rolling Stone’s Music Video of the Year. His third album, “Full Moon Chamber,” arrived July 10 via Atlantic Records, following a run of sold-out headline tours across North America, Europe, the U.K., Asia and the Middle East. He is repped by CAA and Big Bad Wolf India, with Everyday Rebellion handling worldwide management. Gai’s credits include “Three and a Half,” which streams on Netflix worldwide after a stellar festival run; her second film, “Namdev Bhau: In Search of Silence,” played at Busan, BFI London and Palm Springs. Jugaad’s “Last Film Show” was shortlisted for the international feature Oscar. “With Doobna, I wanted to make a film that feels like life right now: real, funny, tragic, chaotic, and impossible to escape, impossible to press a reset button,” said Gai, a Ukrainian native long based in Mumbai. Kanakadandila, whose D36 roster spans South Asian-descent artists in the U.S., U.K., India and Pakistan, framed the film as a response to a gap he sees in how the region’s music culture reaches screen. “India has a singular relationship between music and cinema, but there’s a fundamental mismatch between the spirit of the contemporary scene and the format of traditional Bollywood,” he said. The film is the anchor of a South Asia-focused push within Marginal’s broader international slate, which also includes projects in Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Thailand, Europe and Canada. “This is a trillion dollar market, two billion people, more English speakers than the United States itself, and the fastest growing, digitally connected, and largest youth population in the world,” Sharma said. “Just as we’ve seen Korean culture, food, fashion, music and cinema resonate around the world, a similar wave is coming from South Asia.” Marginal has produced more than a dozen features in just over five years, including Tribeca 2025 Audience Award runner-up “The Rose: Come Back to Me,” Tribeca Jury Prize winner “Cypher,” and the recently released horror title “Camp.” Hudson Williams Confronts Autograph Hounds Who Followed Him Home in Viral Video: ‘Please F—ing Leave’ Future Debuts at No. 1 With ‘The Real Me,’ as Rolling Stones and ‘Heated Rivalry’ Soundtrack Also Bow in Top 10 ‘Heated Rivalry’ Funko Pops Are Here: Shop the New Shane and Ilya Collectibles Ahead of Season 2 ‘Thunder Point’ Heats Up as Fremantle, Bell Media and ‘Sullivan’s Crossing’ Showrunner Bring Robyn Carr’s Next Series to the Global Market: ‘It’s “Friday Night Lights” Meets “Virgin River”’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Heated Rivalry’ Success Sparks New Publishing House From Gay Adult Entertainment Giant Falcon | NakedSword (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Heated Rivalry,’ ‘Industry,’ ‘Widow’s Bay’ Lead 2026 TCA Awards Nominations Loading comments... title: ‘Toy Story 5’ and Theme Parks Power Disney in Latest Quarter, as Company Teases Big Changes Ahead
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All August 5, 2026 3:39am (L-R): Bullseye, Jessie, and Lilypad in Disney and Pixar's Toy Story 5 Disney/Pixar The Walt Disney Co. reported its fiscal Q3 earnings early Wednesday, with films like Toy Story 5 , streaming, and its lucrative experiences division powering its results. The company missed Wall Street expectations for revenue, but beat them in operating income and earnings per share, with stronger-than-expected theme park performance helping to bolster its bottom line. The company also teed up some big changes coming to its divisions, teasing a plan to turn Disney+ into “a comprehensive membership ecosystem,” with the first elements of that vision rolling out early next year. Related Stories Business Disney and TikTok Ink Wide-Ranging Deal, Videos From Tech Platform Will Be Added to Disney+ Movies 'Toy Story 5' Has Given Away 18,000 Toys to Sick Kids Meanwhile, the company’s lucrative consumer products segment will move from being part of Disney’s experiences division and into its entertainment division: “We believe this shift will have strategic and operational benefits by bringing the monetization of our IP through consumer products closer to the studios that create that IP,” the company writes. Disney reported revenue of $25.2 billion, up 7 percent from a year ago, with segment operating income of $5.5 billion, up 21 percent from a year ago. In entertainment, revenues were $11.3 billion with operating income of $1.68 billion. In streaming, SVOD entertainment revenue (Disney+ and Hulu minus ESPN) was $712 million, a sharp increase from a year ago, and a signal that streaming is becoming more reliably profitable. The company did note that The Mandalorian and Grogu and the live action Moana “underperformed” at the box office, but argued that “these franchise investments contributed to value creation beyond their theatrical releases.” Toy Story , for example, has generated more than $16 billion for Disney as a franchise, it said. In experiences, revenues were $10 billion, up 10% from a year ago, with operating income of $3 billion, up 20%. That was despite market concerns around theme parks, especially with Universal recently reporting lower than expected results. The company said that international visitors are still down at its park, but they made up for it with domestic attendance and annual passholders. In sports, the NBA Finals helped power ESPN, with revenues of $4.5 billion, up 4 percent, though operating income fell 17 percent to $858 million due to higher NBA rights costs. Disney also said that it would use the cash from the $1.2 billion sale of its A+E stake to do stock buybacks, and elaborated a bit on how it expects to use artificial intelligence: “With AI, it isn’t simply about efficiency. We use it first and foremost to enhance a creative process that will always be human-centered, artist-driven, and creator-led,” the company writes. “We’ve cultivated the world’s richest portfolio of IP and production experience across a century of filmmaking, giving us an advantage that our peers and no new entrant can quickly replicate.” THR

title: Disney Streaming Profit Doubles in June Quarter, Company Shifting Consumer Products to Studios Division
full_text: Aug 5, 2026 3:36am PT Disney Streaming Profit Doubles in June Quarter, Company Shifting Consumer Products to Studios Division CEO Josh D'Amaro also outlines use of new AI tool for Disney's parks team By Jennifer Maas Plus Icon Jennifer Maas TV Business Writer @jmaasaronson Latest Disney Streaming Profit Doubles in June Quarter, Company Shifting Consumer Products to Studios Division 22 minutes ago Why Parents Are Still Afraid of Video Games After 50 Years and How a Gaming Nonprofit’s New Workshops Are Trying to Help 2 days ago ‘Talking Tom & Friends: World’ Kids’ Mobile Game Launches The Smurfs Crossover (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All ©Walt Disney Co./Courtesy Everett Collection Disney posted mixed results for the June 2026 quarter, as Disney+ and Hulu continued to boost profits and the theme parks division turning in solid performance. And Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro revealed his latest move to restructure the media conglomerate’s operations: He’s moving most of consumer products out of Disney Experiences and into the entertainment unit. In a letter to shareholders accompanying the earnings results Wednesday, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro said that starting in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (which runs October-December 2026) Disney will be moving “much” of its consumer products business results from the experiences segment to the entertainment segment. That means that sales for merchandise for “Avengers: Doomsday,” for example, would fall under entertainment revenue and put the bulk of the consumer products biz under Disney Entertainment’s studios group. The consumer products business accounted for $1.1 billion in revenue this quarter, the strongest year-over-year growth in five years. Related Stories Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God “We believe this shift will have strategic and operational benefits by bringing the monetization of our IP through consumer products closer to the studios that create that IP,” D’Amaro, who previously ran Disney Experiences before stepping into the CEO job in March , wrote in the letter to shareholders. “Additionally, we believe this presentation will better reflect the returns our Entertainment segment is generating from the content it produces and make our Entertainment segment more comparable to peer reporting methodologies.” Popular on Variety On the streaming front, revenue from Disney+ and Hulu was up 11% for the April-June quarter, to $5.53 billion — and operating income in the entertainment streaming segment more than doubled, to $712 million, compared with $329 million in the year-earlier period. Disney said overall streaming subscription revenue was up 15%, to $4.7 billion, and ad sales increased 3%. The company no longer discloses total subscriber figures on a quarterly basis. In the letter, D’Amaro also outlined some AI developments at the company, including the Parks division’s recently implemented large-scale use of Disney’s proprietary AI tool, J.A.R.V.I.S. “We made our J.A.R.V.I.S. AI tool available to our more than 2,000 Imagineers earlier this year, giving them instant access to over 70 years of institutional knowledge,” D’Amaro wrote. “We’re using AI-powered digital twins and simulation tools to design and stress-test new attractions, including leveraging these tools for the Abu Dhabi park. And we’re applying AI to simplify the booking and planning journey for our guests, while equipping our cast members with AI-assisted tools to better serve guests in the moment.” Disney continued to tout the blockbuster success of “Toy Story 5” in the latest quarterly earnings results, revealing the film’s release has also led to the franchise as a whole reaching more than 2 billion hours streamed on Disney+ and record consumer products sales. Overall, Disney reported net income of $2.63 billion on $25.2 billion in revenue, with adjusted EPS of $2.06 (up from $1.51 with the exclusion of income tax and one-time impairment and severance charges) for the quarter ended June 27. Revenue was up 7% year over year while net income increased 28% (without those favorable exclusion, income was down 48%) for the period, which is Disney’s Q3 of fiscal 2027. Wall Street analysts on average forecast earnings per share (EPS) of $1.85 on $25.4 billion in revenue for the three months ended June 30 (Disney’s Q3 of fiscal 2026), according to data provider LSEG. Total segment operating income was up 21% to $5.6 billion. Free cash flow came in at $3.1 billion. Following recent layoffs , D’Amaro noted that Disney remains “highly focused on reducing costs across the enterprise to create incremental capacity to invest for growth and are evaluating a variety of levers, including reductions in labor and SG&A.” The CEO says the company is “mid-stream in this work” and “will provide future updates on our progress.” Previously, Disney had set an $8 billion goal for share repurchases in fiscal 2026, which ends in September. With the confirmation of the sale of Disney’s 50% stake in A+E Global Media to an affiliate of co-owner Hearst, Disney said it will use the approximately $1.2 billion in cash from the sale to increase its total share repurchases for the year to at least $9 billion. Disney took a $812 million impairment charge during the quarter due to its investment in A+E. Severance costs for the quarter were $88 million. Overall, Disney’s entertainment segment (which includes film and TV studios and networks as well as the streaming business) revenue was up 6% to $11.3 billion for the quarter. The division continued to receive a boost from the acquisition of a large stake in Fubo last fall, which it combined with the Hulu live TV business. The addition of Fubo contributed a 4% lift in subscription and affiliate fees revenue, which was up a total of 12%. Ad sales for the entertainment division were down 1% on lower rates. Content sales decreased 6% due to a decrease in TV/video-on-demand and home entertainment distribution sales. On the movie front, Disney praised “Toy Story 5” for surpassing $1 billion in global box office, bringing the franchise’s lifetime global box office to more than $4 billion, while downplaying recent releases “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu” and the live-action “Moana” movie, both of which “underperformed our box office expectations,” Disney said. ESPN revenue for the quarter was up 4% to $4.5 billion. Ad sales increased 5% on higher impressions. Operating income declined 17% to $858 million, a larger drop than the 14% that Disney previously estimated due to a double-digit percentage increase in programming expenses, including the timing of new rights agreements, on the close of the NFL Network deal. “Contributing to the lower-than-expected operating income were four-game sweeps in early rounds of the NBA Playoffs and the impact of a network carriage dispute,” Disney said. Disney Experiences, which currently houses theme parks, cruises and consumer products, saw June quarter revenue of $10 billion (up 10%) and operating income of $3 billion (up 20%). Attendance at Disney domestic parks grew 3% from April-June. Disney World in particular experiencing a “stand-out quarter, with healthy core attendance increases from domestic tourists and annual passholders, and effective summer promotions and new experiences that further supplemented growth,” though Disney notes it has “continued to face headwinds from international attendance at our domestic parks.” For the July-September quarter, the company expects total segment operating income of approximately $4.9 billion, with the inclusion of financial results from a 53rd week of operations. “Our strong fiscal Q3 results and reiterated full-year outlook reinforce our confidence that we are uniquely well positioned,” D’Amaro said in the letter to shareholders. “Decades of IP investment have built deep fan connections that translate into strong financial results. Our accelerating global guests growth at Experiences, ‘Toy Story 5’s’ theatrical and consumer products success, and strong ESPN viewership gains all helped expand our consumer reach this quarter. Together, our results show a unique ability to engage consumers at scale, both digitally and physically, even amid macro uncertainty.” Also Wednesday, Disney struck a content deal with TikTok that will let the app’s creators (initially in the U.S.) make shorts tied to characters and stories from Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars, FX and other properties. title: Eli Roth Admits ‘Ice Cream Man’ Features Generative AI After He “Mispoke” About Using The Technology
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘The Artful Dodger’ Renewed For Final Season At Hulu & Disney+ ‘Baywatch’ Reboot Beaches At Amazon Prime Video Across Europe, India & Canada The Show Will Go On Without Ariana Grande: ‘Sunday In The Park With George’ Producers Plan For Musical Without ‘Wicked’ Star View All August 5, 2026 3:11am ‘Ice Cream Man’ Valerie Flores/The Horror Section Ice Cream Man features a scoop of AI. That’s the revelation from horror director Eli Roth after he admitted to adopting the technology in a “few scenes” of the slasher film, despite initially saying that animated sequences were brought to life traditionally. In an interview on Monday, the Hostel helmer was asked if he used artificial intelligence in Ice Cream Man scenes featuring a Fleischer Studios-style animation that entrances kids and transforms them into killers. “I have an animation background and I drew it,” Roth initially told website Polygon. “I worked with an animation team and I wanted it to look and feel like — there’s an old Mickey Mouse cartoon where he goes to a haunted house and there’s brooms and dancing skeletons and this kind of flowing dancing stuff and the jittery style of the animation. So I drew the loop cycles and the styles. Then I had some animators help kind of make it a little more fluid, and I worked with an artist to give it a bit of an old-timey jittery feel. But I sat there and I drew out the frames that I wanted.” Related Stories News 'Ice Cream Man' Review: Eli Roth Blends 'Home Alone' And 'Hostel' For Over-The-Top Unrated Bloodfest News 'Ice Cream Man' Review: Eli Roth Blends 'Home Alone' And 'Hostel' In Over The Top Unrated Bloodfest In Search Of A Story It was later revealed that Ice Cream Man ‘s credits included a mention of Dark Half, an AI visual effects company. title: ‘The Mummy’ Poster Ads Banned From London Underground After Advertising Watchdog Cites ‘Distressing’ Imagery
full_text: Aug 5, 2026 3:11am PT ‘The Mummy’ Poster Ads Banned From London Underground After Advertising Watchdog Cites ‘Distressing’ Imagery By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Cannibalism Comedy-Horror ‘Ali & Ben’s Spicy Meats,’ Starring Amir Nafis, Signs Abnormal Studios for Worldwide Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 10 hours ago Cate Blanchett, Nina Hoss on the Friendship Driving ‘Elektra/Persona’ at London’s National Theatre: ‘There’s a Lot of Masking and Unmasking’ 14 hours ago Tokyo’s TIFFCOM 2026 Expands IP Market, Adds AI and Anime Conferences 22 hours ago See All ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection The U.K. Advertising Standards Authority has ruled that outdoor poster ads for “Lee Cronin’s The Mummy ” breached its code by presenting an image that gave “a realistic impression of a dead child,” while clearing companion TV and streaming spots for the same campaign. The ASA investigated four issues stemming from several complaints about ads for the Warner Bros Entertainment U.K. Ltd. cinema release, seen in April this year. The regulator upheld one complaint and rejected the other three in a ruling published Aug. 5. Related Stories Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God “The ASA received 30 complaints, many of whom believed the ads were distressing for children and adults,” the ASA said. Popular on Variety Posters on the London Underground and at outdoor sites showed a close-up of a mummified female figure with grey, ashen skin, cracked lips and one eye swollen shut, wrapped in material resembling a shroud and inscribed with hieroglyphic-style symbols. The ASA said the figure’s features gave “a realistic impression of a dead child” and that the material wrapped around her added to that impression. Because the posters ran in untargeted locations, including on the London Underground and at a site visible from a children’s nursery, the regulator concluded the imagery was likely to distress young children who saw it. It ruled the posters unsuitable for outdoor display in that form, finding them in breach of CAP Code rules 1.3 and 4.2. Warner Bros. had argued the poster’s neutral expression, open eye and absence of a sarcophagus or restraints were deliberate choices meant to reduce distress, and noted the studio’s outdoor buying policy of keeping horror titles at least 100 metres from schools – a standard that does not extend to nurseries. The ASA ordered that the poster ads “must not appear in the form complained of” and directed Warner Bros. to keep future marketing likely to frighten young children away from places where they would see it. The ruling cited BCAP Code rules 1.2, 4.1, 4.10, 5.1 and 32.3, and CAP Code (Edition 12) rules 1.3, 4.1 and 4.2. The ASA rejected a separate complaint that the posters trivialized child loss or ongoing global conflicts, finding that text identifying the image as promotion for a film provided sufficient context, even if some viewers found it distasteful. Variety has reached out to Warner Bros. Discovery for comment. The campaign also included a TV ad and a matching Prime Video ad depicting a family receiving a call about a daughter who had gone missing eight years earlier, with the father questioning what she was doing in a 3000-year-old sarcophagus. On-screen text read, “Some Things Are Meant to Stay Buried.” Both ran with a post-7:30 p.m. scheduling restriction cleared by Clearcast. The ASA found the TV and streaming ads were unlikely to cause serious distress and that their scheduling restrictions were sufficient to limit exposure to young children, rejecting complaints that they should have been kept off air later or targeted more precisely on Prime Video. It also noted Clearcast’s data showing an average children’s index of 31 across the TV placements – well below the industry baseline of 100 that represents typical child viewership, indicating the actual child audience was low. title: Disney and TikTok Ink Wide-Ranging Deal, Videos From Tech Platform Will Be Added to Disney+
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All August 5, 2026 3:00am Dan Kitwood/Getty Images TikTok videos will be coming to Disney +. The tech giant and the entertainment giant have inked what they are calling a “first-of-its-kind” content sharing deal, which will allow TikTok videos from Disney fans to live on both of their streaming platforms. The deal bears a striking similarity to last year’s short-lived announcement with OpenAI to fold videos from Sora into Disney+ … but without the whole AI-generated angle. Creators who opt-in to the program will gain access to Disney assets (think photos and videos featuring Disney characters and IP). A “thoughtfully curated” selection of videos will live on both TikTok and in Verts on Disney+. The companies also say that they “will enable best-in-class creators to unlock special rewards and provide them with increased visibility, access to exclusive events and career development pathways,” making it a two-way street of engagement. The partnership will launch in the U.S. in the next couple months, with plans to eventually bring it to other markets. “The best storytellers are fans first,” said Asad Ayaz, chief marketing and brand officer for Disney. “That has always been true at Disney, and today, fans are celebrating our stories in entirely new ways. This collaboration creates a new bridge between the stories we tell and the creativity they inspire, giving creators a bigger stage to share what they’ve made, and audiences more to discover on Disney+ every day.” “Creators are at the heart of everything we do at TikTok. Their creativity extends the life of films and shows into conversations that fans discover and share,” added Dawn Yang, global head of entertainment for TikTok. “Together with Disney, we’re bringing the authentic creator expression of the TikTok community to Disney+, inviting audiences to experience the shared creativity that makes fandom so powerful.” The deal will inevitably turbocharge Disney’s Verts offering, with the company teasing the possibility of creator content there when it launched in March. Vertical video has become a top priority for streamers, recognizing that consumers who watch videos on their phones are just not likely to turn it sideways in most use cases. Peacock, HBO Max, and Netflix have all also rolled out enhanced vertical video offerings in recent months. But the Disney-TikTok tie-up also recognizes the role that creators are playing in fandom, with fand of characters and IP, be it Marvel Star Wars or Moana, often turning to social video platforms to dissect, discuss and celebrate those characters and worlds. title: Disney, TikTok Strike Content-Sharing Deal Aimed at Boosting Short-Form Programming on Disney+
full_text: Aug 5, 2026 3:00am PT Disney, TikTok Strike Content-Sharing Deal Aimed at Boosting Short-Form Programming on Disney+ By Brian Steinberg Plus Icon Brian Steinberg Senior TV Editor bristei Latest Disney, TikTok Strike Content-Sharing Deal Aimed at Boosting Short-Form Programming on Disney+ 1 hour ago Paramount Q2 Profit Dips, With Streaming Boost Offset by TV Declines 15 hours ago Jimmy Fallon is Nearly Last Late-Night Host Standing Amid Summer Hiatus 2 days ago See All Getty Images; Courtesy of Disney Disney is going long on short-form content. The entertainment giant struck an alliance with TikTok that will have creators on the popular quick-hit video service making shorts tied to characters and stories from Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars, FX and more. The resulting pieces from creators who opt-in to the program will be available on both TikTok and on Disney+ in the form of “Verts,” the company’s vertical video products. Related Stories Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread “This collaboration creates a new bridge between the stories we tell and the creativity they inspire, giving creators a bigger stage to share what they’ve made, and audiences more to discover on Disney+ every day,” said Asad Ayaz, Disney’s chief marketing and brand officer, in a statement. Popular on Variety The agreement will launch in the U.S. in coming months, and the companies intend to move it to other markets around the world. Financial terms were not disclosed. It’s no secret that younger people are watching shorter videos with more frequency, including TikTok vignettes, Facebook Reels, even “whip-around” sports shows like NBC Olympics’ Gold Zone and NFL Red Zone. The format is driving conversations around everything from wellness to food to pop culture. Many prominent advertisers are also investing in it, with big-spending companies including Procter & Gamble and JCPenney creating “microdramas” and “microcontent.” Disney has telegraphed its interest for months. It already introduced “Verts” to ESPN’s direct-to-consumer streaming service, and unveiled plans for short-form video to surface on Disney+. “Short form and creative content, they’ve exploded in the past few years, and it’s an area we’re focused on because we have deeply committed fans who, you know, love our brands and our franchises and characters, and they want to engage with them in this new way,” said Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro, speaking during a May call with investors. “This is specifically important when we think about Gen Alpha, obviously, the newest generation of Disney fans. What we’re doing is we’re experimenting with short-form content in a variety of ways.” The TikTok alliance might fill in for a previous ambitious project that was ultimately scrapped. Disney in December unveiled a three-year deal with OpenAI that would have allowed users of the company’s generative-video Sora platform to generate short, user-prompted social videos using a set of more than 200 masked, animated or creature characters from Disney, Marvel, Pixar and Star Wars, as well as costumes, props and vehicles. Disney planned to make a $1 billion equity investment in OpenAI, and receive warrants to purchase additional equity. The project, however, was ultimately scrapped after OpenAI decided to shut Sora down. Now TikTok will help Disney move further into the emerging field. Both companies will administer a “Disney Creator Ambassador Program” that will give certain users incentives and access to events and career development. TikTok creators will gain access to assets related to hundreds of films and series from Disney’s vast library, and fans will be able to take part in a Disney-centered experience on TikTok that will be refreshed regularly. “Together with Disney, we’re bringing the authentic creator expression of the TikTok community to Disney+, inviting audiences to experience the shared creativity that makes fandom so powerful,” said Dawn Yang, global head of entertainment for TikTok, in a statement. There is some hope that allowing Disney intellectual property to fuel TikTok pieces will have a halo effect for Disney’s films and programs. Nearly half of respondents on a survey commissioned by TikTok and conducted by Ipsos, a market-research firm, said that discovering entertainment content on TikTok spurred them to go on to watch a movie or show on a streaming service or traditional TV. In January 2026, under a deal brokered by the Trump administration, ByteDance sold a majority stake in TikTok’s U.S. business to non-Chinese investors , including Oracle, Silver Lake and Abu Dhabi’s state-owned investment firm MGX. title: Edinburgh Television Festival Advisory Chair Adam Hawkins Urges Industry To “Embrace Change” In Confab’s Final Year In Scotland
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘The Artful Dodger’ Renewed For Final Season At Hulu & Disney+ Nimrat Kaur, Roshan Mathew & Pavan Malhotra Star In ‘Job Trafficking’, Prime Video Series About Industrialized Online Scams Fremantle Hires Katie O’Connell Marsh As Global Scripted Chief View All August 5, 2026 3:00am Adam Hawkins is the advisory chair for the final Edinburgh Television Festival Getty, Netflix “If this Edinburgh is all about embracing change and embracing the future, then maybe we should do the same with the festival.” That’s the verdict from Adam Hawkins , the advisory chair of the final ever Edinburgh Television Festival , which is held later this month in Scotland’s capital. In an interview with Deadline, the Netflix UK Director of Documentary Series urged the industry to keep an open mind about the future of the festival, which is in 2027 transferring to Greater Manchester in England after 51 years in Edinburgh. The UK television industry, which gathers annually for the event to talk shop and frequent the local ale houses, remains very divided between those who think moving the venue away from Edinburgh is a disaster given the number of agents, producers and creatives in town for the Fringe Festival in August, and those who say the costs have simply become too high to remain a diary date for many – especially those climbing the ladder. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Books Everything We Know About Netflix's 'This Summer Will Be Different' TV Adaptation So Far Legal Producer Adds Defamation Claim To Lawsuit Against Netflix Over Theft Of Hard Drive Of World War II Espionage Pic 'Fortitude' Basic hotel rooms cost an average minimum of $300 per night, with pricier options nearing $700 during the month, but many producers have come for years and see Edinburgh as a crucial moment to take the temperature of their buyers and counterparts. “I’ve always loved going to Edinburgh,” says Hawkins, who worked for the likes of The Tinder Swindler producer Raw before joining Netflix in 2022. “It’s a great buzzy place at this time of year, but Manchester is also an incredibly vibrant city and I think the buzz will probably be the same.” Hawkins – who saw Jeremy Paxman deliver the annual James MacTaggart Lecture in 2007 during his first visit to the event – is known for greenlighting the likes of Victoria Beckham , Robbie Williams and the upcoming Being Gordon Ramsay at Netflix, and worked on the streamer’s first daily World Cup soccer show, Gary Lineker ’s The Rest is Football over the summer. Hawins concurs with Deadline’s read that the corridors of Edinburgh International Conference Centre provide a unique flavor of the local business. “It feels like you’re in the middle of the British TV industry, like an amazing chance for a snapshot,” he says. “Even though I’m the advisory chair this year, I’m hopeful I’ll get the chance to just wander around, as I do think that there is a moment of taking the temperature and seeing everyone together. That’s the magic, isn’t it?” We were speaking prior to my International TV Co-Editor, Max Goldbart, breaking the news that it might not be curtains after all for Edinburgh. Screen Scotland, the body that represents the interests of the Scottish film and TV industry, commissioned a piece of work earlier this year examining what a new fest might look like. Interestingly, Rowan Woods, the former creative boss of the Edinburgh TV Fest, is leading on the work as an indie consultant. It’s a sign that at least some of the local industry disagrees with the TV Foundation’s decision to move the event and of a desire to keep tradition going. A veteran of the UK biz, Hawkins says no other local or international TV event generates the same “electricity in the air” as Edinburgh and adds that if Manchester can recreate that atmosphere, “Then the [new festival] will be a roaring success.” Final edition highlights Michaela Coel delivered the annual MacTaggart lecture in 2018 So what exactly is Manchester going to follow? For starters, YouTube’s VP of EMEA, Pedro Pina, will be stepping onto the same plinth the likes of Paxman, James Murdoch, Michaela Coel and Mark Thompson have done before. His MacTaggart Lecture, which is considered a bellwether for the state of the industry, will likely talk about YouTube’s increasingly important role in British broadcasting – earlier this year it passed the BBC in monthly audience reach for the first time. The shift towards creators, most of whom rely on YouTube as their platform – will also be a hit topic, especially as many remain concerned how that is upending traditional production. Hawkins says the booking is reflective of the changing shape of the biz – one that has been inundated with consolidation such as the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery saga, disruption from AI and new money-making models. “Being part of the festival is solidifying that they are are television,” he says. “They’re not something else, they’re not outsiders and they’re not the newcomers. They are very much part of the furniture now and it is important TV industry sees that, and it’s important they play their part in that. They’re calling themselves television. We must treat them like that.” Hawkins’ employer, Netflix, has faced the same questions of intention. His response is that “none” of the Netflix commissioning team in the UK is American. “We are knitted into the fabric here, and we spend huge amounts of money,” he adds. “Us being a part of it and me leading on it is reaffirming we are part of the British landscape.” Netflix can, of course, point to the fact that it discovered the Richard Gadd play on which hit series Baby Reindeer was based, during an August in Edinburgh. “We are firmly rooted here, and we are passionate defenders of the British TV industry as well,” says Hawkins. Richard Gadd first performed ‘Baby Reindeer’ in Edinburgh Bar Apple TV, every major broadcaster and streaming spending in the UK will feature across ten Spotlight Sessions, including YouTube for the first time. One recurring criticism with the format is that they can be used a promo sessions rather than substantive content, but Hawkins refutes this, saying media outlets’ hunt for headlines is at odds with what they are actually achieving. “Edgier talking points are not interesting to most TV producers,” he argues. “They just want to know how to sell their next show and how to be successful. I’m hopeful people will leave those sessions with a clearer understanding.” There will also be off record, peer-to-peer sessions to give delegates face time with major commissions, as part of Hawkins’ determination to give producers more access to decision makers. Also notable is the first public appearance of BBC Director General Matt Brittin, a former Google boss who replaced Tim Davie earlier this year. “He has only just got his feet under the table,” says Hawkins. “I am sure he will hit the ground running, so he might have some interesting announcements, but it will be kind of like Pedro in a way – he’s at the ‘getting to know you’ stage. He is an interesting choice as somewhat an outsider to the BBC, and people want to know what he is all about, and what his priorities are. I’m glad he chose the festival.” Before that, BBC journalist Ros Atkins will return for a third year in a row to open the festival on Tuesday, August 25, with his trademark fast-paced, data-driven assertions of issues facing he industry. Further journalism heavyweights Cathy Newman, Susanna Reid and Clive Myrie will discuss truth in an age of misinformation, while Hawkins will introduce broadcaster Amol Rajan for his Alternative MacTaggart. Hawkins will also be on stage interviewing former footballer, broadcaster and Goalhanger co-founder Gary Lineker about the “third act of his career” – quietly building a media empire after spending six weeks with him in Times Square during the World Cup recording the Rest is Football podcast. YouTuber, podcaster and BAFTA presenter Amelia Dimoldenberg – “a TV star who is naturally part of the new generation” – will also be in conversation to discuss on her career and Gary Oldman will receive a Global Icon Award and look back on six seasons of Apple TV cop drama Slow Horses . SNL Masterclass ‘Saturday Night Live UK’ One of the more well-attended sessions will undoubtedly be the SNL UK Masterclass , which will bring together the on-screen performers, producers and Sky commissioning executives behind the show. Initially met with consternation and scorn upon its announcement by a skeptical industry, the remake of the famed NBC sketch show’s first season was broadly considered a success by its ending earlier this year. A second, expanded season has been ordered and Sky is hoping it will become part of the British industry fabric, with many of Season 1’s clippable segments doing the rounds on social media each week after broadcast. Jack Shep, whose portrayal of a smouldering Princess Diana was arguably the viral moment of the first run, will appear on stage alongside the likes of fellow performer Ania Magliano, writer Daran “Jonno” Johnson, lead producer James Longman and Sky unscripted commissioning chief Phil Edgar-Jones. “Even though it is a decades-old heritage brand, it works because of the clips,” says Hawkins. “In some ways, it is clip-first, program-second. It is as much about the new wave of television as anything else. I’m really excited about that.” Amid the excitement around announcements, Hawkins – who is working alongside Edinburgh TV Festival Managing Director Campbell Glennie and new Head of Editorial Niall Flanagan on the event this year – knows there will never have been such apprehension heading into an August in Scotland. Not only is the future south of the border, but the industry is facing unprecedented disruption and a continuing financial problem. “Things are changing, and I don’t think they will go back,” he says. “Some people want to turn the clocks back ten years, but I’m hopeful there will be excitement and that people are up for the challenge. We have the best TV industry in the world, in my opinion, and we can meet the moment. The only way to be right now is up for the challenge, and while there will be nerves in the industry, I’m hopeful this is a nervous excitement. As for how the future in Manchester shakes out, Hawkins – who did not play a role in the selection process – provides an honest assessment. Could, Deadline asks, the foundation that runs the TV Festival look back on this decision in five years and consider it a mistake? “Hard to know,” replies Hawkins. “I have no idea, and the proof will be in the pudding. Honestly, knowing how hard they work on it and how much they care, I’m sure it will be a success.” Hawkins is embracing the change, the question is if the industry embraces it with him. title: Inside ‘I Is Another’: The True(ish) Story of the Man Who Massaged a Nazi and Maybe Saved Lives
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 5, 2026 1:00am 'I Is Another' Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega A few years ago German writer-director Felix Randau ( Iceman ) got what sounded like an interesting proposal from France: to direct episodes of a miniseries about Felix Kersten, the former massage therapist of Nazi SS leader Heinrich Himmler. “When I got back to Berlin and read their concept, I really liked it,” he recalls. “But there was this one special sentence in it that said, ‘If Steven Spielberg had known about Felix Kersten, he would have shot a film about Felix Kersten and not about Oskar Schindler.’ I knew that Steven Spielberg struggled for, I don’t know, about 10 years before he started shooting Schindler’s List , and he’s a smart guy who has a lot of assistance. So I became suspicious and started my own research, going to the archives and reading a lot of books and stuff.” Related Stories Movies Maria Bäck on 'Brave New Love,' Her Provocative Take on Motherhood, Desire and Modern Romance Lifestyle Ariana Grande's Decision to Withdraw From 'Sunday in the Park' Came as Surprise to Key Production Members In the process, he realized that Kersten’s legacy is much less clear-cut. “I figured out that the story the French guys wanted to shoot was a hero story, a superhero story,” Randau tells THR . “But I felt you simply cannot do it.” He soon started focusing his work energy elsewhere. The result is his new film, I Is Another ( Ich Ist ein Anderer ), which world premieres on Friday, Aug. 7 in the Piazza Grande program of the 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland. Set in 1952, the film sees a journalist ambush Kersten and his wife on a train because she has doubts about the heroic narrative that he has been presenting about himself — one that might even get him the Nobel Peace Prize. What starts as a normal interview quickly turns into a psychological cat-and-mouse game. Is Kersten a hero or an impostor? Or could he maybe be both? “Every story has three sides,” Randau says in a director’s note. “Yours. Mine. And the truth…” To explore all these complex themes, I Is Another features a cast of big European names, led by Danish star Claes Bang ( The Square , Bad Sisters , Home ) as Felix Kersten, Austria’s Valerie Pachner ( The Stories , Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore , Four Minus Three ) as journalist Hedda, fellow Austrian Susanne Wuest ( Sound of Falling ) as Kersten’s wife Irmgard, German actor Timocin Ziegler as Hedda’s husband Winfried, and Germany’s Martin Müller as Himmler. Felix Randau, courtesy of Felix Randau The film, whose cinematographer was Sebastian Thaler, was edited by Joana Scrinzi. Beta Cinema is handling international sales. For writer-director Randau, I Is Another is much more than a post-war film — and much more timely. “Of course, it’s a period movie, but it has a lot to do with our present time,” he tells THR . “It’s about truth and the question: what is truth? Nowadays, there are no more fundamental agreements about anything, so truth has become quite a flexible thing. And that’s very dangerous, as we all can see. So, I Is Another is a movie about that.” Indeed, the themes of truth and image that the movie explores seem tailor-made for the social media age. “If Felix Kersten was alive today, he would be deep into all this social media shit, I’m pretty sure,” Randau acknowledges. But he highlights the ambiguities and shades of gray that he sees in Kersten that the writer-director wanted to also showcase in I Is Another . “He was a narcissist. He was an opportunist,” says Randau. “But I think he also was a hero somehow because he saved some lives. Not thousands, as he said, but he saved some lives. And I think he saved lives not for good reasons. He wanted to save his own ass, I think.” Where in the film’s facts turn to fiction doesn’t really matter much, according to the filmmaker, because much of how people feel about Kersten depends on whether they focus on his autobiography or facts and stories told by others. “All the scenes with Himmler and Kersten are from Kersten’s autobiography,” Randau explains. “So they are, I think, all fake, but it is his truth. All the other stuff, the journalist and the train ride and stuff like that, is invented. It’s fiction. But somehow it’s also true.” Director Felix Randau and stars Claes Bang and Valerie Pachner during the shoot for ‘I Is Another,’ courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega Of course, to bring the story of Kersten and the themes that I Is Another explores to life, Randau needed a strong cast. “I’m really proud of our casting,” he tells THR . “They all were great and added so much.” Randau reached out to Bang first to cast him as Kersten. The Danish star had never heard about the massage therapist. “I did not know about any of this until Felix brought it to me, and it’s quite interesting because it seems to be a story that everybody’s quite fascinated by when you retell it,” the star tells THR in a Zoom chat during a break from filming the Netflix series Assassin’s Creed . “It’s a story that’s really gone under the radar, even if it’s a quite crazy one.” The team may have spent quite a few years getting the financing for the movie together, but the actor remained up for it throughout. “Ever since he brought it to me, I’ve been really into it and really wanted to do it,” Bang recalls. “I really felt strongly about this. So I stayed with it, and we managed to make it last summer. We had to do it quite fast because there wasn’t a massive budget. I think we had 24 shooting days altogether, which is a stretch for something like this. Everybody really put in a massive effort. Everybody was so devoted to it, and that is something that I will carry with me.” How did he think about Kersten and what was key for portraying the character? “It’s really hard to find out what is actually the truth here,” Bang observes. “But what’s interesting is that if this guy hadn’t been so preoccupied with his legacy, then we would have had no story to tell. It’s only because it seems that after the war, he was not quite content with the credit he was given for what he had done, and therefore he started perhaps exaggerating.” For the Danish star, Kersten’s story is about the human need for validation: “Ultimately, Kersten wants the Nobel Peace Prize because that would validate him. That whole thing of not being able to just trust yourself and knowing that you have done your bit seems weird and wild.” Claes Bang as Felix Kersten and Martin Müller as Heinrich Himmler in ‘I Is Another,’ courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/Ostlicht Filmproduktion/Wega Filmproduktion The fact that a prominent world leader has been desperately hoping (some might say whining) for a Nobel Peace Prize is not lost on Bang. “Obviously, we have Trump at the moment who is seeking the exact same validation. I mean, he also so desperately wants the Nobel Peace Prize. I know that the parallel is too much. But actually it’s more about … when can we just trust ourselves and know in our hearts ‘I have done my bit.’ Why can’t we just find our inner peace?” Adds Bang: “What intrigued me, and that’s probably also something that I can really relate to and recognize in myself because I really very often wonder, ‘Why do I need that bloody validation from everywhere else? Why do I need the reviews to say that I’m great? Why do I need people to come up to me and say, Wow, that was a great movie.’ Why isn’t it just enough for me just to be whatever I am?” In case you wonder: Bang and his director on I Is Another weren’t at all concerned with him trying to look like the real-life Kersten, which he doesn’t — at all. “That is not the story we’re trying to tell here. We’re trying to tell a story of the journey of a soul,” the star emphasizes. “This is not the wax museum of Madame Tussauds. So that was never important.” Pachner was game for the role of the journalist immediately. “I loved the title, and the film’s themes were something I felt I could really connect with,” she tells THR . “It’s this idea of what you tell yourself and others about yourself, and how that can be very far from the truth. And what is the truth? Felix Randau also plays with our own idea of what’s true and right. And there is this autobiography that Felix Kersten wrote and how people took it as fact just because he wrote it. So, yes, the film is set after the Second World War, but with talk about fake news, it also feels very modern.” Valerie Pachner as journalist Hedda and Claes Bang as Felix Kersten in ‘I Is Another’ Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/Ostlicht Filmproduktion/Wega Filmproduktion She adds that the character of Hedda is more complex than she may appear. “I was really happy to explore that because it felt so rich,” says Pachner. “It’s not this young journalist who is just this good girl who wants to get to the bad guy. She has her own very twisted and dark story. I’m so happy when I get to play a woman where not everyone says, ‘Oh, she’s so nice.'” In fact, Pachner enjoyed teasing that her character isn’t sure who she is or wants to project to be either, very much like Kersten. “As Hedda, I didn’t know who I was,” she shares. “Is me another? Who is I? Or maybe I just want to be different. And I think she really wants to be. That struggle tells us that maybe she and Kersten are not that different.” Pachner had never met any of the other cast members, but she felt a natural chemistry with them once shooting got underway. “We all enjoyed doing the scenes with the four of us, the two couples,” she says. “It just flowed. These weird relationships were kind of there, and there was such a rich history behind Hedda’s relationship with her husband. The Kerstens play these weird mind games with the younger people. I enjoyed working with all of them so much. They’re all really, really great actors.” Wuest was also fascinated by the themes explored by the film, and couldn’t help but notice parallels to our current moment. “I feel that the timing of the film is so spot on for so many reasons,” she says. “First of all, it’s all about the image you create of yourself, and how manipulative that is. It’s like on social media where it’s not only about the ego; it’s about selling something all the time. And the film is about the questions of who do we want to be and how do we want to be perceived from the outside. That has become more important than creating a community, which I think is very toxic. I think it is a dead end.” Director Felix Randau and stars Claes Bang and Valerie Pachner during the shoot for ‘I Is Another,’ courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/ostlicht/Wega She adds that the movie also ties in with a troubling political trend that’s been on the rise throughout the world: “The second thing is the rise of all the right-wing radical politicians and ideologies again, which I think go hand-in-hand with this me, me, me culture. The film tells a story about that and perspective. You have at least three, if not four or five, different perspectives. You have the perspective of Felix Kersten. You have the perspective of the journalist who’s trying to get to him. You have the perspective of his wife. You have the perspective of the poor journalist’s husband. And then you have the perspective of the audience who also has a take on it. Plus, then you have the perspective of the person who tells the story, which is the director. So there are a lot of layers.” Wuest concludes that I Is Another is much more timely than audiences may at first expect: “We live in very strange times, and I think the film covers and mirrors that.” As mentioned before, the Kerstens of I Is Another look nothing like the real-life couple, and Wuest lauds director Randau for “allowing different ideas to happen.” Such as when they were trying out different looks for Irmgard. Says Wuest: “I was putting on makeup, and we were discussing what she could look like. I thought her prime was in the 1930s, maybe in the 1940s even. And people tend not to change hairstyles every decade. We keep the hairstyles we grow up with. And because this story is being told by Felix Karsten, we get to see his memory and his idea of everything. So, Felix Karsten and his wife don’t see each other the way they really look, but more like this Hollywood couple. I really love that the film twists these things and ideas.” THR

title: Locarno Film Festival Head Giona A. Nazzaro Talks Mission To Liberate Spectators In The Age Of The Algorithm As 79th Edition Kicks Off
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Scores Biggest All-Time Middle East Opening Weekend Amid Stunts & Drone Shows Toronto Unveils Wavelengths & TIFF Classics Lineups With Films By Angela Schanelec, Radu Jude, Denis Côté & Lisandro Alonso TIFF Centrepiece To Showcase 54 Features With Kamila Andini’s ‘Four Seasons In Java’ & Avi Nesher’s ‘Our Loves’ Among World Premieres View All August 5, 2026 12:57am L-R: Isabella Rossellini, Giona Nazzaro, Zoe Saldaña and James Gray Getty Images/Michael Buckner/Deadline The Locarno Film Festival opens today with the world premiere of French directorial duo Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh’s The Green Eyes in front of 8,000 spectators on the lakeside town’s Piazza Grande. The opening ceremony will also see Isabella Rossellini feted with the festival’s Excellence Award, with further honorees across the festival including Darren Aronofsky, Virginie Efira, James Gray, Asia Argento, Rick Baker, Zoe Saldaña and producer Sigurjón “Joni” Sighvatsson. Other star guests include Olivia Wilde with her $40M box office breakout The Invite ; Monica Bellucci in the role of the aristocratic mother of a troubled teenager in Giovanni Tortorici’s Luca Guadagnino produced drama Ketticè and Claes Bang in post-WW2 intrigue I Is Another , all of which play on the Piazza Grande. Related Stories News 'Bruton:' Biopic About Man Who Briefly Escaped Prison During 10 Year Sentence Lands Sales Rep Ahead Of Locarno Debut News James Gray To Receive Locarno's Honorary Career Pardo Award With the issue of migration into Europe hitting the headlines this past week after tens of thousands of people attempted to cross without permission from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, The Green Eyes is a timely opening film. Watch on Deadline Set in the Landes in southwestern France, it follows 11-year-old Chaya whose brother goes into a mysterious deep sleep when their family is served with deportation papers. The drama takes its cue from so-called resignation syndrome, a state first observed in Sweden in the 1990s among the children of asylum seekers, which researchers suggested was sparked by trauma and a sense of powerlessness. “The opening film is crucial. It’s like the opening beat of a concert,” says Locarno Film Festival Artistic Director Giona A Nazzaro. “We wanted to share with the audience in Locarno that we’re fully aware of what’s going on in the world, but at the same time that we think we can tackle what’s going on through the tools of cinema, storytelling, imagination and fantasy,” he continues. The Piazza Grande lineup traditionally showcases more accessible fare while independent world cinema competes for the Golden Leopard in the International Competition and edgier works by mainly but not only emerging directors are showcased in the Cineastes of the Present sidebar. Nazzaro says he is not keen on making a distinction between “so-called public films” and “cinema for the highbrow few”. “The real challenge today is to create a possibility where different forms of cinematic art can coexist with the same rights and dignity in the same public space of festival,” he says, adding his dream is to liberate spectators from preconceived viewing choices,” he explains. “It’s a kind of dream to regain cinema as a freedom that can’t be predicted through algorithms or consumer habits… my aim is not to shape the program within the expectations of how cinema should be consumed today but rather create a space where cinema can be experienced as a discontinuation, or an interruption… welcome to Locarno, where your algorithm does not work anymore,” he continues. Nazzaro says the diversity of the Locarno program builds on his work at Venice Critics’ Week, which he headed from 2016 to 2020. “We aimed to welcome new filmmakers in Venice like Helena Wittman ( Drift ), Bertrand Mandico ( The Wild Boys ), Anna Eriksson ( M ), who were completely out of the box back in the day, and now have become, luckily, more established names,” he explains. “What we try to say with a curated diversity is that obviously we have a limited number of slots, but we try to pick differences not only in subjects and stories, but also in the approach to the cinematic form.” He gives artist Beatrice Gibson’s first feature At Night in the Cineastes of the Present, following six women traversing Paris after dark, as an example of a film ticking these boxes. “It’s an outstanding film that tackles issues of identity and power representation, even in contexts and circumstances where you think we have moved on… it is extremely eloquent in the way it points to some of the very crucial crossing points of our contemporary conversations about where we are right now,” he explains. Nazzaro highlights recent Cineastes of the Present success stories such as Sophy Romvari’s Blue Heron , which won Locarno’s First Feature Award, and then played in Toronto’s Centrepiece sidebar, clinching the Best Canadian Discovery Award, and the well-travelled Golden Leopard winner Sweetheart by Margherita Spampinato. “Our DNA has always been about discovering new filmmakers, new talents, new possibilities for cinema. Locarno is one of the places where you can really dive into the possibilities for the art form today,” he says. Under Nazzaro’s watch, Locarno has also welcomed pictures like Sony Pictures’ action-comedy Bullet Train starring Brad Pitt, but in a trend seen across the European festival circuit this year studio pictures are absent at this edition. He suggests it is a sign of the times. “I’m a huge fan of North American cinema and what Hollywood used to stand for. I’m not oblivious to the changes, the industrial, financial, and structural transformation that the whole studio system is going through. I’m not even sure if there is still something like a studio system, not in the sense or way that we used to know it,” he says. “That said, the collective intelligence of the Hollywood system is very much alive and expresses itself through unique artists such as Tom Cruise, and we’re also seeing how the system can work for an auteur like Chris Nolan and The Odyssey .” “It’s always very risky to say definitively what is going on with the studios, because the strength of that system, whatever that system has become, is that it has in its DNA the capacity, the possibility, the opportunity to contradict itself at all times. Just a couple of weeks ago, we were all discussing Backrooms , which I think is extremely brilliant, and Obsession ,” he continues, noting Locarno feted the latter’s executive producer Jason Blum with its Raimondo Rezzonico Award in 2022. The U.S. is represented this year selection by Gray’s Paper Tige r and Wilde’s The Invite on the Piazza Grande as well as Greek American director Erin Vassilopoulos’s New Jersey and New York City-set drama Destroy All Girls in Cineastes of the Present. Restored versions of David Lynch’s Wild at Heart , Kevin Costner’s Dances With Wolves and Martin Scorsese’s Taxi Driver will also play on the Piazza Grande. This year’s retrospective entitled ‘Red & Black – Hollywood Left and the Blacklist’ explores the filmmakers and films who fell victim to McCarthyism. Restored by Zurich-based laboratory Cinegrell in collaboration with the Locarno Film Festival, the new 4K version of Dances of Wolves i ncorporates 30 minutes of previously unseen footage extending its duration to just under four hours. Nazzaro suggests that while Costner’s revisionist Western epic may seem naïve today, it still represents an antidote to current U.S. politics. “It’s like saying, ‘Ok, the hippies in Laurel Canyon were completely naive and stoned out of their heads most of the time but then came the 80s, and I’d rather go with the hippies than with the yuppies. You know what I’m saying?” he explains. Currently tied up with the next instalments of Horizon – An American Saga , Costner is not scheduled to attend, but Nazzaro hopes the late night screening will be a cinephile event nonetheless, with at least a handful of spectators staying to the end in the small hours of the morning “We’re aware of the time but the aim is to create an experience from which people might say, ‘I was there’. We’re not expecting 8,000 people to be there waiting for the sun to come up with the end credits but that’s the idea,” he says. He recalls attending a screening of the 216-minute version of Michael Cimino’s Heaven’s Gate with the director in attendance in Venice in 2012. “The director of the festival in Venice at the time [Alberto Barbera] had this very late night screening and was saying, “Guys, you have to see this film because the film will not be existing anymore. So, it was packed,” recounts. “This is different. We’re bringing something back to life. The idea of going with that kind of film through the night with that kind of length is to say something very simple: you can win whatever night it is we are living through with the light of cinema.” Judge Sets WBD Merger Trial For March; Streaming Fuels Mixed Q2 ‘Brand New Day’ 2nd Fastest To $1B WW; Record U.S. Monday With $47M Female Friends In Their 50s Drive Summer Success Of ‘Five Star Weekend’ & ‘Ride Or Die’ Numan Acar Joins Pic As Kevin J.
