title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Review: Season 4 of Apple’s Hit Soccer Dramedy Struggles to Find Anywhere Interesting Left to Go
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All August 5, 2026 12:00am 'Ted Lasso' Apple TV It would surely take a real a-hole to hate on Apple’s Ted Lasso . As of the latest season — the fourth, following a third that played coy to the very end about whether it might be the last — it remains perhaps the most insistently warmhearted series on television, full of kindly heroes who are open of mind and generous of spirit. Every new person is just a new friend waiting to happen. Every new challenge is an exciting opportunity to extend oneself or someone else a bit of grace. In a world where cruelty so often seems to be the point, it should be a balm for the soul, a fortifying reminder that common decency still matters and always will. Related Stories TV 'Ted Lasso' Makes Long-Awaited Return: When and Where to Watch Season 4 Online TV Meet Coach Alice, the New Face of 'Ted Lasso' Ted Lasso The Bottom Line Sweet but empty. Airdate: Wednesday, Aug. 5 (Apple) Cast: Jason Sudeikis, Hannah Waddingham, Juno Temple, Tanya Reynolds, Jeremy Swift, Brett Goldstein, Abbie Hern, Faye Marsay, Jude Mack, Aisling Sharkey, Rex Hayes Creators: Jason Sudekis, Bill Lawrence, Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly And yet, I must confess, what this latest outing brought up in me was not my better angels but my inner grump, growing ever more impatient with the whole endeavor. Unimpeachably well-intentioned but frustratingly hollow, the long-delayed new season mostly serves to confirm that the Richmond way may have run its course. Perhaps I’m being harsh on a season that, in fairness, I did not actively despise. (I did warn you I was a jerk.) Where season three frustrated with its aimless pacing, its unruly plotting, its self-congratulatory strain of goodness, new showrunner Jack Burditt ( 30 Rock , Modern Family ) dials back the worst of the show’s excesses. The five (of 10) episodes sent to critics average a still-kinda-long-but-basically-reasonable 45 minutes. Our hero’s general vibe has been scaled back from nigh-saintly to merely very nice. All the male players — save Brett Goldstein’s Roy Kent, now Richmond’s coach — have been jettisoned from the show, taking their many half-baked storylines along with them. The problem is that, having rid itself of its messier elements, Ted Lasso has replaced them with…well, not much of anything, really. The season follows Ted ( Jason Sudeikis ) as he takes charge of their inaugural women’s team, none of whose members at this point have gotten ample or interesting enough screen time to leave a real impression. (I’d keep an eye on Jude Mack’s cheerfully unhinged goalie Boots, Faye Marsay’s maternal Lizzie and Abbie Hern’s prickly Gemma, though.) The only new face that does demand a lot of attention so far is a prickly new assistant coach, Alice (an excellent Tanya Reynolds). Seeing as she’s the single most interesting part of the new season — not least because she’s the only lead who’s yet to succumb to the Pluribus -ian hive mind of Lasso-style positivity — it’s easy to want to lend it to her. The challenge to be overcome this time is not some scheming villain or a more talented rival team, but the dully abstract concept of an unjust system: In the face of sexist male fans, skeptical executives, an indifferent sports media and a shameful lack of resources, can Rebecca ( Hannah Waddingham ) and Keeley’s ( Juno Temple ) new passion project of a team possibly prevail? It’s a timely plot, what with the recent surge of interest in established organizations like the WNBA and the NWSL as well as nascent ones like the PWHL and the WPBL , and undeniably a noble one. Ted Lasso knows it, sprinkling in speeches about how much it matters not just for little girls but little boys, older women and really people of all ages and genders to see that women can play, too. (And if you think it strange that such a proudly feminist endeavor has put a man in charge, there’s a whole episode-two subplot explaining, not very convincingly, why in this specific case it’s actually fine.) But it’s one thing to label a thing important. It’s another to make it interesting. Ted Lasso succeeds at the former, but falters at the latter. In keeping the players and fans at arm’s length, at least for now, the show misses a shot to make the stakes feel personal — to show us what makes them so passionate about this sport, to reflect on the paths that have brought them here, to take stock of their own private hopes now that they’ve arrived. It might yet, and I hope it does; for my money, the most fun I had this season was watching these women bond or butt heads with equal raucousness. Mostly, the series’ focus remains on its core cast. But rather than use the in-universe three-year gap to flip to a new chapter in the characters’ lives, it simply returns them to a familiar status quo. Assistant coach Beard (Brendan Hunt) remains trapped in a toxic on-off dynamic with Jane (Phoebe Walsh), despite having married her in the previous finale. Keeley and Roy are “really really good friends” who want to be more, but are kept apart by mechanisms that have only ever existed in the minds of screenwriters desperate to stretch out a will-they-won’t-they. Rebecca’s dragging her feet on a commitment to her hot pilot, Matthijs (Matteo van der Grijn), again seemingly just so the series can milk this storyline as long as it can. As for Ted, Sudeikis still shines most in the moments when we see sadness or worry peeking through his relentlessly upbeat façade. But the creaky pacing of this season — it takes a full episode for Ted to even begin to consider taking the job, all the better to deliver on what I can only assume is a lucrative partnership with Kansas City’s tourism board, and then two more before he’s assembled a full coaching staff and team — can’t hide the fact that the show doesn’t seem to know what to do with him when he’s not giving inspirational, metaphor-laden speeches. Because really, where is there even left for Ted to go? In the first season, he was met with resistance on all fronts to his unorthodox methods of coaching, his ignorance of the sport, his sheer Americanness. By the end of the third, he’d so fully converted everyone to his brand of empathetic leadership that even Trent Crimm (James Lance), his toughest media critic, has written a book touting his wisdom. The Ted that knocks on Rebecca’s door this season is not a fish out of water but a legendary hero returning to a kingdom he’s remade entirely in his image. Ted himself would never say so, of course — he’d aw-shucks the notion via some convoluted reference to a beloved ’80s movie. But he might as well let himself weep, for there are no more naysayers left for him to conquer. THR

title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review
full_text: Aug 5, 2026 12:00am PT ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review By Alison Herman Plus Icon Alison Herman TV Critic aherman2006 Latest ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review 4 hours ago Ariana Grande May or May Not Be Struggling. We Can Talk About It Without Trying to Shame Her 17 hours ago ‘Rick and Morty’ Spinoff ‘President Curtis’ Plays It Safe, but Keeps the Sci-Fi Franchise Cruising: TV Review 1 week ago See All Courtesy of Apple TV Anyone with even the vaguest understanding of the profit motive can understand why Apple TV sports comedy “ Ted Lasso ” has returned three years after its poorly received — yet still widely watched — third season seemed to close the book on its story. A streaming service continuing to milk one of its few major hits doesn’t prohibit the result from being enjoyable; if the first three seasons of “Ted Lasso” are effectively one (overlong, especially toward the end) sports movie, then Season 4 is its perfectly routine sequel. And in a genre filled with redemptive second chances, “Ted Lasso” could use one of its own. If a show has the chance to correct for mistakes like overindulgence and bloat, why not take it? Related Stories Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Season 4 introduces a premise that gives Jason Sudeikis’ titular American-football-turned-British-football coach a chance at both a fresh start and a return to old stomping grounds. Two years after Ted walked away from AFC Richmond and took his signature mustache back to Kansas City, team owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), marketing chief Keeley (Juno Temple) and operations head Leslie Higgins (Jeremy Swift) arrive stateside with an offer he can’t refuse: coaching the club’s brand-new women’s team, who begin their existence as the underdogs — specifically, Greyhounds — their male counterparts once were. Given the cultural bias against women’s sports leagues, they’ll likely remain so even if they succeed. Popular on Variety The concepts of class reunion (Ted goes back to London and gets the gang back together!) and clean slate (Ted takes on a new challenge!) are somewhat at odds. Sure enough, Season 4 is far more enjoyable as the latter than the former — even as “Ted Lasso” keeps privileging nostalgia and tired subplots over its best chance at a renaissance. Tanya Reynolds of “Sex Education” is a welcome addition as Alice Chilton, a coach whose constant scowl and clipped severity make her a well-suited foil for Ted’s sunny optimism until she inevitably warms to it. But, at least in the five episodes provided to critics out of an eventual 10, she’s pretty much the only new character who feels fully established, because “Ted Lasso” refuses to make room in the ensemble by sidelining (or is it touchlining?) old ones. Like Sudeikis, actor Brett Goldstein remains a creative force behind the camera, which may explain why his churlish then player, now coach Roy Kent remains such a presence despite the pivot away from his men’s squad. But while foregrounding Rebecca and Keeley makes sense given the renewed focus on women in sports, Roy and Keeley’s on-again, off-again romance lost its allure several seasons ago. Figures like Roy and Ted’s longtime deputy Beard (series co-creator Brendan Hunt) would be better deployed as occasional cameos, yet they remain load-bearing — and space-occupying — protagonists. The consequences can border on the absurd: a major decision by Ted’s ex-wife Michelle (Andrea Anders) is sped through rather than shown from her perspective; an episode hinges on a team problem with cliques that’s only depicted onscreen far too late. Until then, we’re mostly told about it by other characters with longer tenures. Contributing to the sense of overcrowding is an otherwise welcome development: no single episode of the first five clocks in at over an hour, the way so much of Season 3 did. “Ted Lasso” is not for everyone; the blindingly earnest social consciousness and relentless positivity some find so grating remain firmly in place. (Feminist commentary was never the series’ strong suit, and centering the women’s team prompts more of it than ever.) But Season 4 reigns in some excesses and offers glimpses of fresh new faces: a walk-on player who’s also a single mom; a goalie who refuses to wear gloves; a new mentor for Rebecca, played by comic legend Tracey Ullmann. If only the show would clear the field for them. ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review Production: Warner Bros. title: Jason Sudeikis Sets Up ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4: “It’s Getting Back To Doing What He Loves”
full_text: Skip to main content By Rosy Cordero Rosy Cordero Associate Editor, TV @SocialRosy More Stories By Rosy Rebecca Rittenhouse Cast In Hulu’s Cable Guy Pilot ‘Colin From Accounts’ Sets Premiere Date For Third & Final Season Mary Holland Joins DC’s Jimmy Olsen ‘Superman’ Spinoff Series View All August 5, 2026 12:00am SPOILER ALERT: The following reveals major plot points from Apple TV ‘s Ted Lasso Season 4 premiere. It’s been more than three years since we caught up with Ted Lasso ( Jason Sudeikis ) and all his fabulous friends and loved ones back in Season 3. Following a hiatus, the Apple TV series Ted Lasso is back, and it’s like he was never gone. Well, almost. When we reconnect with Ted in Episode 1, he’s back in his hometown of Kansas City, after leaving his life in London behind to be closer to his son Henry (Grant Feely). Ted is now working at Fowch’s Fine Foods, a local grocery store, ringing people up at the register. Related Stories News 'Ted Lasso' Season 4 Release Schedule: When Do New Episodes Come Out? News Juliette Lewis On If 'Cape Fear's Crystal Or Max Is "More Psychopathic," Martin Scorsese's Lasting Support & Season 2 Hopes: "We Will See" Unbeknownst to him, three people from his past are coping with the heat outside his house: Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), Leslie ( Jeremy Swift ), and Keeley (Juno Temple). When Ted sees them, he opens his front door and does a leap into the air (photo below), sharing his joy over their reunion. Famished, Ted takes the trio to a local BBQ spot where they pig out and catch up on what they’ve been up to. Amid the small talk and Rebecca spilling BBQ sauce all over her delicates, she reveals the real reason they are there: she wants Ted to coach their new women’s team. Ted is a little surprised but not really, and a little unsure of how to respond to her generous offer. Jason Sudeikis as Ted Lasso in Apple TV’s ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 After catching Henry’s soccer match, Rebecca, Leslie, and Keeley head back to the U.K. without Ted, who declined the coaching job offer. However, all hope is not lost. When he gets home, he looks at all his mementos from the Richmond days and reminisces about those moments amongst friends. Taking a shot in the dark, he texts his ex Michelle (Andrea Anders), who is with Henry, and both agree to join Ted for a new adventure in England. Ted is chuffed to bits at the prospect. “When we first meet him, he’s really just dad-ing it up. He’s taken a part-time job, and he clearly didn’t blow the money he made while being the head coach of a Premier League team for three seasons. He’s hiding out a little bit, and slowly puts the pieces together of a different way to go about this familiar situation from the inside out,” shared Sudeikis with Deadline, which can be seen in the video above. He added, “So then it’s getting back to doing what he loves, which he was depriving himself of for one reason or another. That’s open to interpretation. I have my theories.” Even though Ted is going back to coaching, this will be his first time training women. The team, which viewers will officially meet next week in Episode 2, consists of Boots (Jude Mack), the cheeky twin sisters Niamh (Aisling Sharkey) and Siobhan (Rex Hayes), Margy (Mercedes Assad), and her girlfriend Mady (Annelise Heywood). There will also be a few other new faces that will be introduced in Episode 3. Before Ted arrives in England, the ladies will have been trained by Assistant Coach Alice Chilton (Tanya Reynolds), a lovely and devoted leader who lacks self-confidence. Jeremy Swift, Hannah Waddingham, Juno Temple and Jason Sudeikis partake of the BBQ in Kansas City Of the new experience of working so closely with the women on the team, Sudeikis remarked, “Coaching women for the first time in his life… arguably, he has a complicated relationship with women. He’s certainly not practiced in mentoring and coaching. It’s similar to being a fairly new father of a young girl; you don’t necessarily know what to do, what you can do, what you’re allowed, what’s appropriate…” Sudeikis later added, “Because I was once a boy and I’ve, at this point in this journey, not been a girl, I’m guessing a lot of times. Girls are very good at making you wonder while you’re guessing, which I appreciate at this point in my life. I think Ted, for a guy who lives in the questions, is getting answers from areas he never expected.” Earlier in the episode titled “Home,” while still in Kansas City (Missouri or Kansas, you decide), Leslie took a break from the group to visit the American Jazz Museum. Unfortunately, it was closed for a private event. Lucky for him, there was another option right next door: the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum. The gentleman selling the tickets convinced Leslie to consider his second choice. Not really being into baseball, Leslie was hesitant, but he went in anyway. He learned a lot about some of the greatest Black players of all time, with a large focus on Satchel Paige. Swift commented on the scene, “It’s an unexpected journey because he wants to go to the jazz museum, and it’s a little lesson for him about struggle in sport and overcoming it. Big shout out to Milan Carter, who I did the scenes with, who is just a really beautiful actor, fantastic. I loved working with him. Also, a big shout out to Declan Lowney, who directed that first episode. He’s been on the show since the beginning, and he’s a superb director. A lot of fun to work with.” For anyone planning to visit Kansas City, both the American Jazz Museum and the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum are real institutions that can be visited. Next week, Ted crosses the pond. title: Gregg Sulkin Says “It Took Three Seconds” To Return To Mason Greyback For ‘Wizards Beyond Waverly Place’ Finale: “All I Had To Do Was Look At Selena”
full_text: Skip to main content By Katie Campione Katie Campione Senior TV & Labor Reporter @katie_campione More Stories By Katherine Idaho College Murders Doc Series Grabs Attention On Netflix; ‘Ransom Canyon’ Season 2 Off To Slow Start Jewish Film Institute Reveals 2026 Grant Recipients & San Francisco Jewish Film Festival Award Winners ‘Stranger Things,’ ‘Bluey’ & ‘The Pitt’ Dominate Streaming TV In H1 2026; Peacock Rates High With Unscripted Originals View All August 4, 2026 11:03pm Wizards Beyond Waverly Place Disney SPOILER ALERT! This post contains details from the final season of Wizards Beyond Waverly Place . Gregg Sulkin can rest easy knowing there’s a universe out there where Alex Russo and Mason Greyback are still together. “I mean, I think, in my heart, Alex and Mason are always endgame,” he recently told Deadline after a brief role reprisal as the fan-favorite werewolf and Alex’s former flame for the Wizards Beyond Waverly Place conclusion. “So, storyline wise, I think it’s more in the heart than on the page, and I think all the fans around the world will resonate with that,” he added. “But, of course, delighted to be back on the show. Delighted to work with Selena again. It’s very special to be on back on set in my first American home.” Related Stories News 'Wizards Beyond Waverly Place' Season 3 Release Guide: How Do The Episodes Roll Out? News 'The Devil Wears Prada 2' Achieves Biggest Live-Action Movie Premiere On Disney+ & Hulu Since 'Deadpool & Wolverine' Sulkin makes a delightful, if limited, appearance in the second of four episodes alongside former co-stars Selena Gomez and Jennifer Stone, also known as Alex’s human best friend Harper Finkle. Watch on Deadline As viewers know by now, Wizards Beyond follows Alex’s daughter Billie (Janice LeAnn Brown), whom she shares with former dark wizard Damian Penwulf. But that’s in the real world. In this world, Alex is still living with Harper and is dating Mason, who Harper believes is about to stop by with plans to propose. But, when he gets there, he reveals something else. Mason can’t propose, because he’s dead. Through Mason’s revelations, we learn that Alex has been in some sort of limbo state after throwing herself through a dimensional rift to save her family at the end of Season 2. He and Harper are there only to guide her back to her family. “I felt like there was only one person who was going to do that, and thankfully, they chose Mason,” he said. “I think Mason has always been Alex’s rock.” It’s been more than a decade since the Wizards of Waverly Place finale, and still Sulkin supposes “it took three seconds” to slip back into character. “All I had to do was look at Selena, and it was like, ‘Okay, cool, we’re back,'” he said. “I think, when you have such a special bond with people on a professional and personal level, it’s very easy to slip back into it.” Wizards Beyond has brought back many of the characters from the original Disney Channel series, which ran from 2007 to 2012, so it has always begged the question of whether these important characters would return in some capacity. While Alex and Mason were dating at the end of Wizards of Waverly Place , the continuation establishes early on that Alex has married someone else. Wizards Beyond follows Alex daughter Billie (Janice LeAnn Brown), who she shares with her husband and former dark wizard Damien Penwulf. In large part, the series follows Billie as she unwittingly works to help make her family whole again. Whatever the canon may be, Sulkin remained open to returning throughout Wizard Beyond ‘s short three-season run and had an inkling that the writers would find a way to eventually make sense of a return for Mason. “It was just a matter of fitting in the perfect slot for my character to come back, whilst also giving space for the new show to breathe, whilst also paying respect to my character, [and] Selena and I’s characters’ relationships,” he continued. He hoped the stars might align. “And thankfully, they did.” It’s certainly a brutal end for a beloved original character, but luckily in this universe death doesn’t feel quite so permanent. “I think the amazing about wizards, and when you’re dealing with magic, is that anything can happen,” Sulkin reassured audiences, adding “this was a a chance to say goodbye for now.” He says he’ll “never say never” to future opportunities for Mason’s return, should the franchise spawn again. “The show gave me so much, so I feel like it would be very inconsiderate of me to not want to return the favor to the fans and also the channel for believing in me.” Judge Sets WBD Merger Trial For March; Streaming Fuels Mixed Q2 ‘Brand New Day’ 2nd Fastest To $1B WW; Record U.S. Monday With $47M Female Friends In Their 50s Drive Summer Success Of ‘Five Star Weekend’ & ‘Ride Or Die’ Numan Acar Joins Pic As Kevin J. title: Maria Bäck on ‘Brave New Love,’ Her Provocative Take on Motherhood, Desire and Modern Romance
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 4, 2026 11:00pm 'Brave New Love' Courtesy of Snowglobe Swedish-Danish writer-director Maria Bäck ( I Remember When I Die , Psychosis in Stockholm ) likes to push the envelope. With her new feature, Brave New Love , she invites us to talk about love, relationships and desire — but not within the tidy bounds of what’s considered “normal” or “right.” The film centers on Kate, a mother torn between her husband, Orla, and a secret relationship with another man, Andreas. A triangle of madness? Of sadness? Of badness? Something else entirely? Watch and decide for yourself. Brave New Love stars Kathrine Thorborg Johansen ( Post Mortem: No One Dies in Skarnes ) as Kate, Simon Sears ( Shadow and Bone ) as Orla, young Noemi Carbone Mannov as their daughter Athena, Anders Danielsen Lie ( Sentimental Value , Everybody Digs Bill Evans ) as Andreas and Angeliki Papoulia ( Dogtooth , The Lobster ). The film world premieres Sunday, Aug. 9, in the main international competition at the 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland. Related Stories Lifestyle Ariana Grande's Decision to Withdraw From 'Sunday in the Park' Came as Surprise to Key Production Members Lifestyle Fashion Keeps Debating John Galliano. It's Ignoring Its Jewish History. Produced by Anna-Maria Kantariusand and featuring cinematography by Maria Von Hausswolff, Brave New Love was edited by Julius Krebs Damsbo. Reinvent Yellow is handling international sales. Ahead of the Locarno premiere of the film, Bäck talked to THR about the inspiration for Brave New Love , why she enjoys asking tough questions, working with a cast of actors who have made names for themselves and why the film’s title reminds you of that famous Aldous Huxley novel. What was the inspiration for Brave New Love ? My interest in all kinds of normative questions has been something that’s been following me forever. I have, for the last 30 years or so, been either in or out of relationships, and my friends have been in or out of relationships. So it’s this huge collection of dilemmas and problems with love life, which has always been something that interests me. I’m also fascinated by how hard it is for people to confront habits. That doesn’t only apply to love, but when you study something like love, which is so present in our lives, many of these things become very clear because we always struggle with love. And not so much has changed regarding the rules of love in modern times. When I think about what drove me to make the film, I keep returning to this want and need to share a loneliness and the feeling of “being fundamentally wrong.” It is so human to fuck up; we all do it all the time! And you can feel empathy with — almost — anyone if you understand their inner world. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe The film doesn’t come across as a recommendation though… Yes, the film is not trying to say that you should have an open relationship. I don’t have an open relationship. I live very conventionally in many ways, but it’s just interesting how we can feel like we are very liberal and open, but when we are confronted with reality, things turn out to be different. When you hear of a woman like Kate, a mother who falls in love with another man, most people will have a strong opinion. Even though we might consider ourselves liberal, we all have these [ingrained] ideas, and there is shame — so much is about shame. I think all these ideas and feelings are deeply rooted in us. We just have all these predefined and automatic reactions, and we tend not to question them much or update our worldview. This human contradiction is just fascinating and amusing to watch in a way. It’s stimulating to explore that with a story and characters, because there’s a lot to dig into. The only thing I really didn’t want with the film was to create something convenient about love that we’ve already seen before. A love triangle is one of the oldest themes, and I really wanted to challenge that narrative, both story-wise and conceptually in terms of the film’s language. For me, it’s always about questions rather than answers. I feel I know nothing. I just question and doubt everything. I found myself going from laughing to cringing and thinking, “No, don’t do this!” It was a rollercoaster of emotions. How did you write and “build” the movie and its world? I worked on this project for six years, so it’s been a long, long process. Like with all my films, usually it starts with an emotion and an abstract universe that tries to become more concrete. In my head, these themes and this character kept circling around. I write a lot and there was a poem I wrote where I pictured this woman. So she came to me. I didn’t know it was Kate back then. But the first picture I had was this naked woman in a cave watching a man, and I didn’t know who she was. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe So then you connected her to the themes you were pondering? Yes, it becomes an investigation, kind of. Of course, I am in charge because I write, but I also feel a lot that I’m following something that I’m trying to understand. Who is she? Where does she come from? So, things usually come to me in the form of different images, different situations. And I also always collect things from my own life that I find fascinating or provocative or just beautiful, and they make it into the film. Such as a balloon scene, for example, in Brave New Love . My son was playing with this balloon when I was hoovering, and all of a sudden the balloon did something I had never seen. That became a little note and then a scene. Some things come from really concrete stuff like that, and other things come from more abstract feelings that I need to translate. Did you get any help in the writing stage? What I want to mention about the writing process is my collaboration with Eskil Vogt ( Sentimental Value , The Worst Person in the World ), who was my script consultant both on Psychosis in Stockholm and Brave New Love . His humorous and generous mind has meant a great deal for the process in terms of asking me disturbing and provocative questions that helped me shape the film. I work a lot with different methods for different stages of writing — sometimes very open and flowy, and then periods with lots of lists and dots and arrows and stuff that I translate into pretty basic, traditional storytelling. But a guide for me is always a strong desire to surprise and do what you don’t expect. I think that is important. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe You mentioned shame. I also want to ask you about guilt. There are scenes where I can imagine viewers saying, “Kate is a bad mother. How dare she?!” How difficult is it to write something so different from the traditional all-loving, all-caring mother? That’s one of the biggest challenges. I didn’t want to make a film that I had seen before. And I didn’t want to make a film that was convenient. Kate was pretty obvious to me as a character from the beginning, and I knew that I had to defend her. You always apply for money, and from the start, it was very clear that it was provoking to people that she was a mother, and she still insisted on her desire, instead of just putting a lid on everything. People asked me why I even wanted to tell this story because, “She’s so egoistic, and the audience wants somebody they can sympathize with.” So it comes back to me in the sense that I have to work with my own shame, and I have to work with my own willingness to be vulnerable in these kinds of situations. Luckily, this is also something that triggers me in a creative way. I get provoked by the people who get so provoked. If they have this idea that a mother should be a very specific way, that makes me angry. So then it’s easier for me to find the energy to stand up for Kate. And people like Kate exist in real life… Yes, I think this idea that you should change as a person just because you become a parent is so ridiculous. Of course, you change a lot of your values. But why would you stop having the same kind of desire and emotions just because you have kids? It’s easy to say about Kate that she should say goodbye to one of the men, or she should get a divorce, blah blah. Or people would also say she has to be honest and tell her husband. But she knows that her husband doesn’t want to know, so then what? Or if she has to get a divorce, that would mean even more pain for everyone. But I have no good answers. And I wanted to make a film where there were no good answers. It’s not a proposal or recommendation — like, “please come and live your life the way Kate does.” She’s struggling a lot. It’s not something I would suggest. But these things and situations happen. I know a lot of Kates, and I know a lot of Orlas, and I know a lot of Andreas. All these perspectives are all around us all the time. So why wouldn’t we see them in a film? Maria Bäck, courtesy of Leo Bäck Geertsen What’s up with all the Greek references and themes in the film? The daughter is named Athena, there is a Greek island, and there seem to be some references to Greek mythology. That’s a good question. I absolutely love Greece, and I’ve done so all my life. I was a very strange, lonely kid in many ways. And Greek mythology really meant a lot to me. Through cassette tapes, I listened a lot to Greek mythology on my Walkman. Even as a kid, my interest in mythology started. It’s just an interest in stories, basically. And then on top of that, I’ve been to Greece a lot in my life, both as a kid on holidays and also later, and I have always felt at home in Greece. I cannot explain why. Even though the film is not about me at all, I use a lot of my own fascinations, so it just came naturally to me to include it in Kate’s character. I’m not romanticizing ancient Greece, but it’s interesting to see how they built Christianity and other cultures on top of it. ‘Brave New Love’ Courtesy of Snowglobe When Locarno unveiled Brave New Love for its lineup, I immediately wondered if it was a reference to Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World . And when I watched the film, I did notice that this title was indeed not a coincidence, right? How early did you know the title? The title I actually had pretty early. I think it was in the first or second draft of the script. I read the book as a teenager, and it made a huge impression on me. I haven’t read it again, actually, but I still have a strong feeling from it. This whole idea of how much society forms our ways of acting and our desires is the core element, of course, of Brave New Love . Of course, it’s a very loose reference. The book works with this very dystopian world where desires are controlled. So I thought what would happen if you had a protagonist who just follows her desire without any restrictions? There is also a scene where Orla is reading that book. Do you know what you will work on next? I’m very early in developing my fourth feature. In parallel, I’m actually expanding Brand New Love as a novel. THR

title: Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 11:00pm PT Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes The second year of Open Doors’ Africa focus takes in new projects and emerging directors and producers from fest and lab winners to new propositions By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest Locarno Open Doors 2026: Next Gen African Tales of Miraculous Snowfalls, Lost Dreams, an African Keyboard Prodigy and New Heroes 5 hours ago San Sebastián New Directors: Billy Lumby, Marlene Emilie Lyngstad, ‘Money Heist’ Star Jaime Lorente and More 6 days ago Mubi to Release ‘La Mesías,’ From ‘La Bola Negra’ Cannes Best Director Winners, in the U.K., Germany, Canada, Australia and Beyond (EXCLUSIVE) 6 days ago See All 'A Vineyard for a Lobster' Courtesy of Talemwa Pius Magic realist love story “Chapa 100,” absurdist political allegory “A Vineyard for a Lobster” and cross-continental queer drama “Hibiscus by the River” look like some of the potential standouts at Locarno’s talent-deep, wide-ranging 2026 Africa-focused Open Doors , unspooling on-site at Locarno over Aug. 5-10. Winner of a 2025 Atlas Workshops Development Award no less, moving from observational social realism to – literally – flowering magical realism, love story “Chapa 100” is set in Mozambique capital Maputo. It marks scribe-helmer Ique Langa ’s follow-up to “The Prophet,” a 2026 IFF Rotterdam main competition entry. Related Stories Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Beginning with an impossible snowfall blanketing a drought-ridden Ugandan village, “A Vineyard for a Lobster” signals the feature debut of Ugandan Talemwa Pius, a New York Film Academy alum. Popular on Variety Now in advanced development, “Hibiscus in the River” is one of five projects brought to market at Locarno by David Ikeata at Vox Cinematic Films, a burgeoning force on Nigeria’s new film scene. Screenings this year at Open Doors pack a particularly powerful punch taking in, for example, Suzannah Mirghani ’s Venice Critics’ Week premiere “Cotton Queen,” a Thessaloniki’s best film and Doha Audience Award winner and the first feature-length fiction film from Sudan that is written and directed by a woman. Also on show is “Crocodile,” a doc-feature best film, Viewpoints laureate at Tribeca Film Festival, New York and Youth Jury Prize at the U.K.’s Sheffield DocFest, and “Diya,” a 2025 TIFF Centerpiece title praised by those who caught it. Aymar Esse’s touching “My Father’s Kora” world premieres at Locarno. A Snapshot of Africa’s Upscale Film Scene Carefully curated, Open Doors 2026 provides a telling take of the range of current upscale titles coming out of Africa plus their artistic and industrial trends. Though light years from parity in Africa at large, women cineastes feature prominently at Open Doors, dominating its producers, new Open Doors Connect and directors sections. Also, “the cohort of Open Doors 2026 is made up of projects and filmmakers that don’t compromise with authenticity,” says Suzsi Bankuti, head of Open Doors. Many titles are indeed redolently and proudly local. “I Live in V.I’s” “character ensemble and dramatic situations are colored with different aspects of the Nigerian collective psyche,” promises director Ugochukwu Azuya. In “Crocodile,” Nigeria’s The Critics collective, though achieving increasing global renown, debate what it takes to be a Nigerian filmmaker. Directly or indirectly, most films deal with the state of Africa today. That includes a critique of post-colonial dynamics. Formally, the British Empire et al. has gone. But their legacy lingers. In “Cotton Queen,” set on a Sudanese cotton farm, teen Nafisa, raised on her grandmother’s heroic tales of battling British colonizers, sets out to save the cotton fields – and herself when a British businessman arrives planning to introduce genetically engineered cotton. “‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’ grows out of my interest in how colonial structures continue to shape authority, belief and communal life in Uganda decades after independence,” explains director Talemwa Pius. Facing Africa’s Challenges It Takes a Village, a panel at Locarno Pro on Aug. 8, will examine new investment cinema models. Africa desperately needs them, crippled by a fundamental lack of traditional national film funding incentives. Open Doors does hint, however, at some ways African cinema can go and indeed is going. One is the full international co-production and sales agent route, empowering a production with top technical talent. One case in point: Produced by Caroline Daube’s Strange Bird in Germany and Didar Maneki’s Maneki Films in France and co-produced by Annemarie Jacir’s Philistine Films in Palestine and Jordan, “Cotton Queen” was set up as a Germany, France, Palestine, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Sudan production, supported by 10 institutions in those countries and Netherlands’ Hubert Bals Fund. African companies are not just looking towards Europe, however. At Locarno’s mass networking encounter Match Me!, Amadeu Alban at Brazil’s Movioca is currently in development on two Brazil-Nigeria projects, “Trapped” and “La Pyramide,” reflecting his strategy of building co-productions across the Global South. Or filmmakers are turning to genre, with its ingrained entertainment drive. Brought to Open Doors by producer Tapiwa Chipfupa, “Life On the Other Side of the Sun” has supernatural elements; “Diya” weighs in as a blood money crime thriller. Pius uses genre storytelling “to reclaim African narratives and expand how the continent is represented on screen,” he says. Open Doors producer David Ikeata’s slate at Vox Cinematic Films spans “fiction and genre-driven storytelling,” he notes. Rather than a market ploy, however, that passion can come from the filmmakers themselves. “Crocodile” charts how Godwin and Raymond, not yet 11, create a homemade collective with siblings and cousins, shooting ever more ambitious sci-fi films on one of their dad’s iPhones. Or companies can seek out larger same-territory entities, galvanized by global streamer deals. Nemsia Studios, one of Nigeria’s leading film production-financing companies which signed a slate deal with Prime Video in 2022, has boarded Ikeata’s “Hibiscus by the River” as a financing partner. Such deals may be for the lucky few. Their tenor is clear, however. A new initiative, Open Doors Connect, bringing together producers from Africa, Latin America and Asia, aims “to move co-production, circulation and long-term collaboration beyond traditional industry schemes,” Bankuti says. Larger collaboration, now being essayed by film industries as established as France and the Nordic States , is the bigger major way Africa’s film industries can also go. Open Doors 2026 Selection Open Doors 2026 is focused on African projects, producers and directors from outside the northern Maghreb and Egypt and South Africa. Open Doors Projects “Accept My Plea for Burial” (“Baryo Aas Iga Gudoon,” Mohammed Sheikh, Djibouti, Somalia, Qatar) After Warmooge, 12, falls to his death while playing with Waasuge, a fellow goatherd, the village elder fails to resolve the case via customary law and religious counsel. From Minnesota-based U.S.-Somali filmmaker Sheik’s follow-up to “Barni,” screening at Locarno, “a morally complex story where there is no clear truth, told through a rarely seen Somali cultural framework,” he says. ‘Chapa 100’ Ique Langa “Chapa 100” (Ique Langa, Mozambique, Portugal) Sitóe, 80, a Maputo flower vendor, and Valentina, a widowed vegetable seller, fall in love. When he is killed by a speeding minibus when trying to help her, flowers begin to bloom within the vehicle. “My love letter to Maputo, ‘Chapa 100’ is ultimately a story about love, memory, and the invisible bonds that connect us and to the places we call home,” Langa tells Variety. ‘I Live in V.I’ “I Live in V.I” (Ugochukwu Azuya, Nigeria) One of the first titles from Lagos-based Ensemble, launched by Azuya and O.O. Ogunsola last year, a social class satire from Azuya, whose short ghost story “Swimming in a Sea of Trauma,” played IFF Rotterdam. Florence, 23, to avoid a tough commute to her job in luxurious Victoria Island, squats in an abandoned high-rise, a relic from an ‘80s government building project. “A film about grief, urban alienation and gentrification in the city of Lagos exploring the lost hope of the Nigerian dream,” say Azuya and O.O. Ogunsola. “The Ones With the Tempered Flowers” (Neema Ngelime, Tanzania) Ngelime’s debut feature, a diary-like essay, she says, using constructed archives, cinema verité performances with her family and stop motion to explore, respectively, Neema’s 1990s childhood, today and imagined future. An auto doc feature about “a journey I am taking,” “exploring identity and the expectations of womanhood,” says Ngelime. Produced by LBx Africa, run by creative producer Bramwel Iro and director-producer Sam Soko. “Too Much Music” (Aseye Fiagbe, Ghana) A music doc bio, about Kiki Gyan, a Ghanaian keyboard prodigy catapulted to international fame as a teen with Afro-rock pioneers Osibisa, which he left over conflict over credit and ownership. Shaping African disco and funk, but unrecognised, he became famed for addiction and an early death. “Kiki’s story is about memory and erasure, about who gets remembered for their work and who is remembered only for how they fell,” says Fiagbe. ‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’ “A Vineyard for a Lobster” (Talemwa Pius. Uganda) Billed as absurdist political allegory, after mysterious snowfall blankets a drought-stricken Ugandan village, a desperate trader, a disgraced priest and a reluctant chairman exploit the “miracle.” Their escalating ambitions threaten to tear the community apart. From Kampala-based Gripmagic, “in the film, an impossible snowfall in a Ugandan village becomes a political allegory, echoing colonial intrusion,” says Pius. Producers Tapiwa Chipfupa , Ambidextrous Pictures, Zimbabwe, “Life on the Other Side of the Sun” Heading Ambidextrous, founder of AVEL and Girls Making Films training programs and a producer exploring “implications of tradition, culture and custom within modern-day Zimbabwe and on the continent, particularly in the life of women,” says Chipfupa. One case in point:“Life On the Other Side of the Sun, ” a supernatural thriller set in a men-ruled mountain hamlet which slides into desperation and witch hunts – until the free-spirited girl Sungano emerges as the village heroine. Natasha Craveiro , Korikaxoru Films, Cabo Verde, White Mask (“dja branku dja”) “In a market dominated by advertising, we established an auteur cinema production house as an act of resistance and cultural affirmation,” Craveiro says of Korikaxoru Films, set up in 2017. Following on multi-prized docu-fiction fest fave Pirinha (2024), she is now developing hybrid feature “White Mask” which plumbs what she calls her father’s “identity denial:” “a Black man from Cabo Verde who served as a soldier in the Portuguese army and, after the war, erased his Cabo Verdean life to settle in Portugal as a judge.” David Ikeata , Vox Cinematic Films, Nigeria, “Hibiscus by the River” Set up in 2024 by Nigerian actor Chimezie Imo and producer David Ikeata, Vox Cinematic Films slate includes “Hibiscus by the River,” the tale of a young Nigerian man who moves to England to pursue an education, only to find himself pulled back into the currents of his past. Holmes Awa, behind Prime Video’s “Soft Love,” directs. South African producer-screenwriter Paballo Molingoane, and Bulgaria’s U.K.-based Teodora Shaleva also produce. Mamounata Nikièma , Pilumpiku Production, Burkina Faso General secretary of the Africadoc Association Burkina over 2009-2014 and honored at the Pan-African Film and Television Festival of Ouagadougou, Africa’s largest cinema festival, in 2021. Behind multiple doc-features, such as “Djeliya, Memory of Mandingo,” an ambitious, five-county co-pro. “Our vision is to become a national and continental reference in film production, digital marketing, and promotion, championing impactful African storytelling, creating jobs for professionals, and nurturing emerging talent,” Nikièma has said. Rua Osman , Helomur Picture, Sudan, “Manageable Matter” Osman’s Helomur focuses on stories that explore memory, identity and social transformation, while fostering meaningful South–South and international co-productions. At Locarno with her “Manageable Matter,” a film take on Berlin-based Emma Waltraud Howes’ installation, staging a procession of the Paradox Crew as an Artichoke Brigade, feature nine performances. These build a “meditation on repetition, collective endurance and the search for humility and grace within seemingly unresolvable cycles,” the synopsis reads. Adja Soro (Studio KÄ, Ivory Coast, “Unchosen”) Behind Abidjan’s animation Studio KÄ and now Studi KÄ France and editor-in-chief of Spark Anim and developing African stories such as YA animated thriller series “Unchosen.” It turns on Esmel, an Olympic taekwondo silver medal winner who returns home a national hero, but, linked to his father’s unsolved murder, risks everything in a live TV interview, to help him find his missing sister. “Through Esmel’s journey, ‘Unchosen’ explores the violence of public exposure in a world where the line between good and evil grows thinner every day,” says Soro. Open Doors Feature Screenings “Barni” (Mohammed Sheik, U.S., Somalia) Sheik’s debut feature, a 2025 Red Sea Fest competition world premiere line-produced by Kadir Harbi at Minneapolis-based Aleel, now behind “Accept My Plea for Burial.” Sheik’s passion to depict Somalia through a Somali lens plus older generation fecklessness shines through as Amini leaves her somnolent village to find sis Barni, 9, in a big city. Arrestingly shot – whether ochre scrub-desert or a big city scrap yard beach – speaking well of Sheik/Harbi’s larger production ambitions. “Catcher” (aka “Wrestlers,” Derhwa Kasunzu, Burkina Faso, France, Democratic Republic of Congo, Saudi Arabia) When Kelekele Lituka, a wrestler who became world champion in 1974, dies in 2021, he’s buried with little fanfare. To honor him, the New Generation wrestling club announces one last catch event in his honor, despite a war-torn Kisangani and the fact its members are getting on in years…. A “lovingly made film,” said an IDFA description. ‘Cotton Queen’ “Cotton Queen” (Suzannah Mirghani, Germany, France, Palestine, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan) An undoubted Open Doors standout, sparking some rave reviews – “a beguiling mix of magic-realist fable, coming-of-age drama and post-colonial critique,” says Eye for Eye – scoring top plaudits at a slew of festivals labs such as Cannes’ Cinéfondation L’Atelier and sales from Totem Films to MAD Solutions/Film Clinic Indie Distribution (Arab-speaking countries), TAPE Collective (U.K./Ireland) and Jip Film (Germany). Cotton Queen “highlights how Sudanese girls must navigate authority in all its forms, whether patriarchal or matriarchal – from the specter of colonialism, to familial authoritarianism to the needs of contemporary capitalism,” Mirghani has said. “Crocodile” (The Critics, Pietra Brettkelly, New Zealand, Nigeria) Built on footage collected by The Critics, a kids’ collective filmed over 13 years through 2025 as Godwin, Raymond, not yet 11, launch The Critics, a filmmaking collective based out of a hardscrabble part of Kaduna, Nigeria, making sci-fi and super-hero films. Now, still determined to make Nigerian genre, they’ve received a digital camera from J.J. Abrams and Morgan Freeman’s narrated Ogun Ola: War Is Coming.” “Crocodile” The Critics and New Zealand’s Brettkelly, whose “A “Flickering Truth” played Venice and TIFF and “Yellow Is Forbidden” Tribeca, chronicle together that journey. “Diya” (Achille Ronaïmou, Chad, France, Germany, Ivory Coast) Rated by critics who have caught it – TIFF’s in-house review calls it “a relentless thriller” – “Diya” sees Dane, an NGO driver, accidentally knock down and kills a child, whose family demands an exorbitant blood debt – a diya – driving Dane ever deeper into crime. Ronaïmou’s feature debut, a critique of diya, still widely extended in Chad, in a film praised for its moral complexity, engrossing tension and sense of place. Bought by Canal+ and a triple winner at the Brussels Intl. Film Festival. ‘My Father’s Kora’ “My Father’s Kora” (“La Kora de mon père,”Aymar Esse, Benin, Switzerland, Germany) A Locarno world premiere. Souleymane, an Afro-German trans man, talented fashion designer and increasingly less timid figure on Berlin’s ballroom scene, travels to Dakar to repair his father’s kora. In doing so, he repairs himself, building his new identity rooted in part in his origins, his griot family in Dakar. Souleymane’s journey’s is sluiced by simple but touching scenes such as his bonding with his brother sewing and with grandfather praying and metaphorical shots of the wash of the ocean on Dakar’s beaches. “The Prophet” (“O Profeta,” Ique Langa, Mozambique, South Africa, Qatar) Preaching in the village of Manjacaze, his inspiration and congregation dwindling, evangelical Pastor Hélder turns to black magic to fire up his oratory and heal his parishioners. His powers come at ever larger sacrifice, literally. Pointedly framed, even in vertical box aspect, bringing sense and sensitivity to shots, a black and white film parable becoming “an expression of the community [Manjacaze] that inspired it,” marking out Luque as a director to track. “Katanga: the Dance of the Scorpions” (“Katanga la danse des scorpions, Dani Kouyaté, Burkina Faso) Last caught by Variety at Abidjan’s SICA, debating African cinema’s future , here vet Kouyaté (“Sia, the Dream of the Python”) re-imagines “Macbeth” in Africa, shot in bold black and white and placed in a broadly modern setting. A Fespaco Yennega Etalon d’Or winner, creating many new scenes, but key plot beats and the broad parable of overweening ambition remain. title: ‘The Blacklist Was a Plague’ — Locarno Retrospective Curator Ehsan Khoshbakht Talks About What We Can Learn From the Intolerance of the Past
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 11:00pm PT ‘The Blacklist Was a Plague’ — Locarno Retrospective Curator Ehsan Khoshbakht Talks About What We Can Learn From the Intolerance of the Past By John Bleasdale Plus Icon John Bleasdale Guest Contributor Latest ‘The Blacklist Was a Plague’ — Locarno Retrospective Curator Ehsan Khoshbakht Talks About What We Can Learn From the Intolerance of the Past 5 hours ago Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s Answer to Comic-Con, Sees 3% Rise in Attendees 9 months ago Hideo Kojima Talks ‘Death Stranding 2’ and the Importance of Connection: ‘It’s Not Connection With Headshots and Shooting Each Other’ 9 months ago See All Dalton Trumbo in '10 Hollywood Commie Writers Arraigned' Courtesy of UCLA One of the most shameful episodes in Hollywood’s history is being examined in a new retrospective to screen at the Locarno Film Festival : Red & Black: Hollywood Left and the Blacklist. Speaking to Variety , the retrospective’s curator, Ehsan Khoshbakht , speaks about the inspiration for the program, which features the work of directors, writers and stars such as John Garfield, Joseph Losey, Dalton Trumbo , Dorothy Parker, Richard Wright and Charles Chaplin . Related Stories Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread What was your starting point for the retrospective? I have often wondered why someone who could have lived a life of comfort would instead fight for the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War, as the screenwriter Alvah Bessie did. Or why filmmakers such as Joseph Losey and Cy Endfield at the height of their success would leave their families, and end up working in Mexico, England or Italy, often forbidden even to use their real names. Trying to understand that inner compulsion — not to name names — became the starting point. Popular on Variety ‘España otra vez’ written by Alvah Bessie Courtesy of Mercury Films Did you see contemporary resonance in your program? My reaction was to intolerance and hysteria in the arts. This is not a right-versus-left program. It’s about what happens when the media are abused and misused; when smear campaigns and fear-mongering prevail over rationality and dialogue. There were films such as “Salt of the Earth,” whose Mexican actress was forcibly removed by immigration officers in the middle of production and deported. The blacklist caused serious health problems, tore families apart, drove people to suicide, and prevented some potentially great films from ever being made. It was a plague. So, it is a bitter irony that 80 years later, Dr. Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment the other day. Is it ever going to stop? Every film in the program responds in some way to one of the ugly excesses of the world now, and to the destructive policies of the current administration in the U.S. I didn’t select the program according to that criterion. It is just a painful and frightening coincidence. How did exile change the way the filmmakers worked? They were forced to adapt to filmmaking modes and industries that were alien, smaller and less streamlined. This introduced what I see as a brilliantly eclectic combination of European style and taste with American sensibility and dynamism. Losey’s “Stranger on the Prowl,” with its unusual and effective blend of neorealism and the man-on-the-run theme, is one example among many. Jules Dassin explored his previously unexamined fascination with the psychosexual. Both filmmakers went on to contribute to a modern cinematic language that could not have developed in America. Others, like Bernard Vorhaus, simply crashed out. ‘Mission to Moscow’ by Michael Curtiz Courtesy of BFI/Warner Bros. What films are you particularly excited about? I’m excited about some of the films for various reasons: some because they are key blacklist films that hadn’t been screened before, even in major retrospectives. For instance, the pro-Soviet and frankly embarrassing “Mission to Moscow,” which is a Hollywood film that depicts Stalin as a fair-minded, brilliant leader! Then there are some films that haven’t been screened in this particular context, such as “España otra vez,” the first Spanish film made under the Franco dictatorship to deal explicitly with the Spanish Civil War from the point of view of the defeated side — the Republicans. It’s in the program because it was written by and starred one of the Hollywood Ten, Alvah Bessie. ‘The Intimate Stranger’ Courtesy of BFI Another super-rare film is “The Intimate Stranger,” by Joseph Losey. Perhaps, the most self-conscious meditation on the blacklist. This film was impossible to show for decades. Losey’s son, Gavrik, will be in Locarno to introduce it. There are nearly thirty 35mm prints in the program, and for some of them to be seen in original format is a chance of a lifetime. The retrospective seems to hold a special place of esteem in Locarno among festival-goers. Other contemporary festivals allocate their worst venues to classic films, if they show them at all. Locarno gives us their best venue, the superb GranRex. I cannot think of any other film festival in the world that would allow me to select 50 titles — mostly in 35mm prints — edit a book of newly commissioned essays by leading scholars from around the world, and produce a podcast. I think it matters to our director, Giona Nazzaro , to go deeper into the history of cinema. He’s an avid cinephile. As for our partners, UCLA Film & TV Archive, Cinémathèque suisse and the BFI have all provided us with essential support. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. The 79th Locarno Film Festival runs over August 5-15. title: How Genesis Is Using Korean Hospitality and the Power of Sports to Build a New Kind of Luxury Brand
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 10:23pm PT How Genesis Is Using Korean Hospitality and the Power of Sports to Build a New Kind of Luxury Brand By Katie Ann Lehman Plus Icon Katie Ann Lehman Latest ‘Bluey’ Fans Can Now Bring the Heeler Family Home With Tonies’ New Collection – Here’s Where to Shop 1 week ago Who Will Take Home the Claret Jug? Here’s How to Watch The Open Championship 2026 3 weeks ago From ‘Happy Gilmore’ to ‘Top Gun,’ Golf Apparel Brand Pins & Aces Taps Into Pop Culture Favorites for Bestselling Golf Gear 3 weeks ago See All Genesis If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. A few months ago, crowds lined the 18th green at The Riviera Country Club in Pacific Palisades, California, as 26-year-old American golfer Jacob Bridgeman secured his first PGA Tour victory at the 2026 Genesis Invitational. But the tournament wasn’t just drawing golf fans. Around the course, guests wandered through hospitality lounges, sampled Korean-inspired food and beverages, explored the latest Genesis vehicles and settled in to watch the action from premium viewing areas. Related Stories Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread Disney's Next Big Thing: Malachi Barton on 'Camp Rock 3,' Doomscrolling on TikTok and Not Hiding His Faith in God Genesis may have cornered the golfing market, but their activation at recent events is the kind of experience that’s becoming increasingly common across sports. Today’s biggest sponsorships are about far more than logos on a leaderboard or a name on a tournament. Brands are creating experiences that bring consumers into the action, turning fans into customers long before they ever make a purchase. Popular on Variety T-Mobile , for example, has expanded its sports strategy well beyond traditional sponsorships. The company helps power everything from broadcasting to on-site operations at sporting events. But for fans, the partnership is experienced in more tangible ways: discounted tickets, access to exclusive Club Magenta lounges at events like the PGA Championship and other member-only perks that make for long-term Luxury automakers are taking a similar approach. Mercedes-Benz, for example, has built a strong connection with consumers through Formula 1, where the sport’s focus on performance, engineering and innovation naturally aligns with the brand’s identity. For newer luxury brands, sports sponsorships can serve as a powerful way to start building the recognition that legacy brands already have. Genesis entered that same competitive space in 2015 as a new luxury automaker. Without the history of its established rivals, the brand looked to sports—particularly golf—as a way to create deeper connections with consumers. Why golf? The sport offered a natural overlap with the audience Genesis wanted to reach, their executives tell Variety, from business leaders and global travelers, to luxury consumers who value premium experiences. As the first Official Vehicle and Mobility Sponsor of the PGA Tour, Genesis has embedded itself into events including the Genesis Invitational, Genesis Scottish Open and as well as emerging made-for-TV formats like TGL. The strategy has coincided with rapid growth, with the brand surpassing 1 million global vehicle sales and reaching a record 82,331 U.S. vehicles sold in 2025. The decision to commit to golf early in the brand’s journey was intentional, according to Jose Munoz, President and CEO of Hyundai and Genesis Motor North America. “At the beginning, partnering with the PGA Tour and with Tiger—and committing to golf consistently—was a big decision for us,” Munoz tells Variety. “Back then, we were selling just a few thousand vehicles, and today we’ve achieved record sales and significant growth. We cannot be happier with everything we’ve done together, and the partnership has become not just strategic, but also personal.” That long-term approach is perhaps most evident in the experience Genesis has built around its tournaments. Drawing from the Korean concept of sonnim , or treating guests as honored visitors rather than customers, the brand has reimagined hospitality as more than traditional VIP access. At events like the Genesis Invitational, that philosophy comes to life through thoughtfully designed lounges, elevated food and beverage offerings and welcoming spaces that encourage guests to linger rather than simply pass through. That philosophy carries into the vehicle itself. I spent a week behind the wheel of the Genesis GV70 SUV, and those same priorities showed up in the details. On a long drive from Savannah to Augusta, the driver’s seat massage function became a small but memorable touch that made hours on the road feel effortless. Combined with customizable mood lighting, a quiet cabin and technology that felt intuitive rather than distracting, the experience reflected the same attention to comfort and hospitality I’d seen throughout the tournament. It reinforced something I hadn’t considered before: the sponsorship isn’t just about putting Genesis in front of consumers—it’s about creating a consistent brand experience wherever someone encounters it. Whether that’s relaxing in a hospitality lounge overlooking the 18th green or settling in for a four-hour drive, the feeling is intentionally the same. Across industries, more brands are recognizing that familiarity is one of the most valuable assets they can build. The companies that stand out aren’t always the ones with the longest history—they’re the ones that consistently create experiences people remember. Genesis Fan Shop Genesis is not just showing up at events — the brand is also partnering with brands on must-have merch and apparel that’s become as coveted as a seat behind the wheel. title: Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation
full_text: Aug 4, 2026 8:48pm PT Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation By Jack Dunn Plus Icon Jack Dunn Latest Perez Hilton: Disturbing Livestream Frightens Fans, Rushed to Hospital After Police Investigation 7 hours ago Geno Segers Apologizes For Transgender Comments After ‘Hadestown’ Exit: ‘I Recognize the Impact of My Statements’ 1 day ago Mary Rivera, ‘Spider-Man: No Way Home’ Actress, Dies at 82 1 day ago See All Getty Images Local police were dispatched to the Miami home of Hollywood gossip journalist Perez Hilton after receiving reports about a disturbing livestream during which Hilton, covered in blood, appeared to be cutting himself, Variety has confirmed. The Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office received multiple calls about Hilton’s livestream on Tuesday night and sent deputies to respond. Once on scene, officers spoke with several of Hilton’s family members. Authorities confirmed that Hilton was alone in his home during the time of the live stream. Deputies have since been ordered to “tactically disengage,” but continue to keep an eye on the situation. Popular on Variety “In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritize de-escalation by creating time, distance, and opportunities for communication,” the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said in a statement. “Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimize the risk of injury to the individual, deputies, and the public.” “We are aware of the concerning content circulating online involving our client, Perez Hilton. At this time, we have not been able to make direct contact with him, despite our ongoing efforts to reach him. Our primary concern is Perez’s health and well being, as well as the well being of his family. Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further,” Golden Artists Entertainment CoCEO’s Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan said in a statement when Variety reached out for comment. “We appreciate everyone’s concern and ask that his privacy be respected during this time.” Hilton launched his career in the early 2000s, operating a popular celebrity gossip blog that offered a biting, unfiltered look at some of Hollywood’s most unsavory moments. In a 2012 sit-down with The New York Times , Hilton said that he was no longer aligned with his provocative reporting. “What’s important for me is not being liked, but it is that people think I am no longer toxic to the world,” he said. title: ‘The Odyssey’ Extends Run At Alex Theatre After Becoming Highest-Grossing 70MM Exhibitor Who Had Not Screened A New Movie In 35 Years
full_text: Skip to main content By Armando Tinoco Armando Tinoco Staff Writer @armietinoco More Stories By Armando ‘The Odyssey’ Extends Run At Alex Theatre After Becoming Highest-Grossing 70MM Exhibitor Who Had Not Screened A New Movie In 35 Years Samantha Morton On Why She “Hasn’t Worked For A Year” Since ‘The Odyssey’ & Why She Was “Sad” & “Hurt” After Getting “Fired” From ‘Her’ Ariana Grande Says Upcoming Break Was “Not A Reactive Or Impulsive Thing” & Something Planned Although “Boundaries, They Need To Be Set” View All August 4, 2026 8:25pm Matt Damon and Zendaya in 'The Odyssey' Universal Pictures Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey continues to break records, and now the highest-grossing theater exhibiting the film in 70mm is extending its run. L.A.’s historic Alex Theatre will continue to exhibit the fantasy epic through August 20, 2026, following audience demand. The Odyssey was the first-run movie at the theater since Terminator 2: Judgment Day in 1991 — 35 years ago. The theater recently underwent systems upgrades, including the installation of 70mm film projectors, which welcomed audiences to the special engagement of The Odyssey on July 17. “We’re incredibly grateful to the people of Los Angeles and to film lovers from across Southern California for making our presentation of The Odyssey in 70mm such an extraordinary success,” said Miles Williams, Artistic Director of the Alex Theatre. “The response from audiences has been overwhelming and a wonderful reminder of how much people still value the shared experience of seeing a great film together.” Williams continued, “I’d also like to thank Universal Pictures for recognizing the important role historic theatres continue to play in Hollywood’s cinematic legacy and for partnering with the ALEX to be part of this landmark release. We’re honored to have been part of bringing this film to audiences, and we look forward to welcoming them back for many more unforgettable movies.” Watch on Deadline Nolan’s The Odyssey is close to crossing the $1 billion mark in the global box office, sitting at $911 million after three weekends. The filmmaker shot the entire film in Imax 70mm, which made moviegoers seek the large screens to experience the movie how Nolan intended. title: Big-Bucks-Generating Disney Consumer Products Unit Shifts To Studio Umbrella
full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp , Dominic Patten August 4, 2026 8:02pm In Disney ‘s second corporate shift to the entertainment tent in six months — and just before CEO Josh D’Amaro leads its Q3 earnings report tomorrow morning — the company unveiled plans to to move its revenue-rich Consumer Products division. The shift seeks to create “cohesion across the entire Disney ecosystem and extending the relevance of our franchises for generations,” according to a joint memo today from Thomas Mazloum, chairman, Disney Experiences and Alan Bergman , chairman, Disney Entertainment Studios. To that end, Disney Consumer Products will travel from the Experiences division to Disney Entertainment — specifically under the company’s Studios umbrella. Related Stories Executives Dana Walden Unveils Her Disney Entertainment Leadership Team Spanning Film, TV, Streaming & Games; Debra OConnell Upped To DET Chairman News Disney Closes $1.2 Billion Deal To Sell A+E Global Media Stake To Hearst “Disney Consumer Products will shift the majority of its businesses to Disney Entertainment, sitting within the Studios, beginning October 2026,” the C-Suite duo wrote. “This evolution reflects how these businesses operate today and strengthens that model by more directly linking our consumer products businesses with the creative and business teams behind the content.” The duo said the reorg was a “work in progress.” Watch on Deadline Essentially putting the people who create Disney’s IP in the same room as the people who create products based on that IP, the synergy may not be sexy, but it sure as Hell is a very big deal — if for the sheer size and cash involved if nothing else. DCP-licensed products did $63 billion in retail sales in 2025. With about two months to go before it all is locked in, details are scant about who the internal merger of sorts will work. We do know that Lisa Baldzicki, who was named DCP prez in the spring, will continue in her role. Baldzicki succeeded Tasia Filippatos as the latter became President of Disney Parks International just after D’Amaro became CEO in March. On a practical level, today’s DCP announcement looks to be the rare case of a corporate meld where the amount likely redundancies — read: layoffs — is minimal. Today’s move marks the second time this year a division that used to sit under now CEO D’Amaro in his former Disney Experiences capacity has shifted to Disney Entertainment. Sean Shoptaw, EVP, Games and Digital Entertainment’ and his entire’s division moved over in March . Of the new partnership between DCP and the company’s content creators, Mazloum and Bergman observed, “At its best, this work happens when storytelling, commerce and experiences come together from the very beginning, creating cohesion across the entire Disney ecosystem and extending the relevance of our franchises for generations.” Disney Consumer Products is the world’s top licensor. DCP, today’s memo notes, is “outperforming its nearest competitor by nearly three to one.” The rest of the top five is made up of Authentic Brands Group ($36 billion), People Inc.($27 billion) NBCUniversal ($20 billion), and Hasbro ($17.5 billion).
