title: What David Ellison Is Really Up to
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All August 4, 2026 7:54pm David Ellison, CEO of Paramount, speaks onstage at the Paramount Pictures presentation at The Dolby Colosseum at Caesars Palace during CinemaCon on April 16, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. A raft of pro-merger pieces have appeared in news outlets in the past week. Gabe Ginsberg/Getty Images At first it just seemed like a happy coincidence — a Hollywood agency mogul supporting a Hollywood corporate merger. Ari Emanuel published an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal last Tuesday saying David Ellison buying Warner Bros. was a good idea and that those 12 Democratic AG’s who have sued to stop the deal were on the wrong warpath. “The attorneys general should drop this case and get back to enforcing the laws as they are written,” the WME chief wrote, as he extolled a Paramount -WB tie-up and said it would be good for the business. Sure, Ellison had committed last year to pay Emanuel’s TKO nearly $8 billion to broadcast UFC fights, a fact he conveniently neglected to mention. And the timing certainly benefited Ellison — earnings were coming, a time when Wall Street would be paying close attention and could express its worry financially about a deal falling through. But still, just a nice little stocking-stuffer under the mogul’s tree. Over the past week, though, the support has started to look a lot less like passive presents and a lot more like an active strategy. The play? Make it seem like a lot of Democrat-approved personalities have no problem with the merger, isolating as regulatory crazies Rob Bonta, Tish James and the rest of the dozen AGs suing to block the deal. Never mind that these are some of the country’s most decorated legal enforcers, with many decades of experience, from places as different as Arizona and Massachusetts. The maneuvers unfolded like a stunt pilot’s careful course-plotting. A few days after the Emanuel op-ed came an anonymously sourced story Friday in the Journal about how one of the preeminent national Democratic leaders, California governor Gavin Newsom, was behind the deal foursquare, according to “people close to the suit.” “Newsom’s office has encouraged Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office, which has independent authority to file such suits, to find a resolution out of court,” the paper said. Never mind that Newsom has a long history of deferring to giant corporations (remember his 11th-hour capitulation to Big Tech on Scott Wiener’s AI bill in 2024?) — this merger was going to create jobs! (“State employment would suffer” without a deal, the paper said Newsom has told colleagues, never mind that no credible economist has supplied such evidence.) Another happy coincidence. Or, given that the paper was pointedly not citing sources close to Newsom, perhaps part of an Ellison-led strategy. Then today, an op-ed of Ellison’s own in a redoubt of mainstream liberalism, The New York Times. The mogul trotted out all the usual arguments for legacy media mergers these days — if we don’t do this the tech companies win, movie theaters should survive, Hollywood should be employed. “What I can promise is the work, and more of it,” he wrote , using the noun four times, which is four times more than he used the noun Donald Trump. Los Angeles County researchers have concluded that the merger will likely lead to less work . Meanwhile, Ari has been hitting the hustings, appearing on CNBC Tuesday morning to rattle off a series of Ellison talking points and praising the mogul. “This is a guy who said ‘hey I’m going to make 30 movies a year, 45-day release,” Emanuel said. “He’s gonna spend he says 30 billion in content a year. We need that for the economy of Hollywood.” The comments wouldn’t have been out of place on the Paramount investor earnings-call Tuesday, where executives touted all these numbers and used words like “pro-competitive” to describe the deal. If there’s one thing we know about capitalism, it’s that combining two major companies leads to more competition. These media hits that aimed to buck the headwinds even involved a literal plane — the day Bonta and the AGs were suing, Ellison jetted to Washington to lobby for a federal tax credit, a news stunt meant as much to lobby support among Hollywood as to win over legislators. One story his coverage play overshadowed that week: ProPublica’s bombshell report that Paramount allegedly provided gifts to FCC commissioners reviewing the deal. More of these pieces are no doubt coming, perhaps even in my own outlet. More foot soldiers arguing for the merger’s value to the business, or the world, or the First Amendment. Never mind that the WGA — those fierce opponents of free expression! — have just sued to stop the deal. Doesn’t the world’s richest family have the right to own CNN? Isn’t that enshrined in the Constitution? All these enlisted authors are a shrewd flyer, and you need to give Ellison’s team credit for landing it so effectively. But you also don’t need an advanced radar beacon to see what’s happening. Having courted MAGA and Donald Trump to win the deal federal approval (how many Kennedy Center boxes and UFC ringside seats can one centibillionaire’s son fill?) Ellison is now pivoting to Dems to take care of the state challenge. Not regulatory-minded Dems, as that group, from Elizabeth Warren to Cory Booker to Adam Schiff, have all been sharply critical of the deal and ask hard questions about combining the country’s third and fourth biggest pure-play entertainment companies. Not those decorated and often landslide-winning Democratic AGs, either. But if you get enough Dem-ish poobahs like Newsom and the Kamala-donating Ari on your side, maybe people won’t notice all the Democrats who aren’t. Or enough of their constituents will lose interest, causing AGs to do the same. Heck, maybe people will even magically forget that no fewer than 1,000 creatives, from Bryan Cranston to J.J. Abrams to Glenn Close to Lin-Manuel Miranda, all signed a letter this spring opposing the deal, noting how a merger “would further consolidate an already concentrated media landscape, reducing competition at a moment when our industries — and the audiences we serve — can least afford it” and lead to “fewer opportunities for creators, fewer jobs across the production ecosystem, higher costs, and less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.” Who can remember any of those beloved entertainers’ warnings when an agent is telling us something is good for creativity? There’s a reason Paramount needs the deal to happen. Warner Bros. Discovery turned a profit of $1.2 billion this past quarter once you strip out all the money they had to pay as part of the acquisition (like severance costs). That’s a lot of profit for a company like Paramount, which revealed Tuesday that in the same quarter it netted $41 million . And there’s a reason Paramount needs the deal to happen soon. Starting Oct. 1, Paramount must pay Warners shareholders $7 million every day until the deal closes. By the second week, they’ll have wiped out all the profits they earned this quarter. By the spring, they’ll have wiped out the profits of the company they’re buying. One can’t imagine a lot of joy on Melrose, then, when the word came down Tuesday that the trial won’t start until March . Also, the deal is partly bankrolled by Larry Ellison and his significant AI investments. And can that boom go on forever? The reality is the AGs may not just have the law on their side — they have the leverage. And with every week that passes they have more of it. (With even more come potential Democrat victories in November.) Could they extract a major settlement — possibly even forcing a carve-out of CNN? Don’t rule it out, no matter how many UFC fights Ellison attends with the president. “Winning comes down to having the best stories,” Paramount CFO Dennis Cinelli told investors on the earnings call Tuesday. Ellison and his allies will keep telling them. That doesn’t mean it will result in victory. THR

title: Police Respond to Perez Hilton’s Miami Home After He Appeared to Harm Himself on Livestream
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 7:47pm Perez Hilton Ethan Miller/Getty Images Police reportedly responded to Perez Hilton ‘s home in Miami after the celebrity gossip blogger appeared to be harming himself on a TikTok livestream. In graphic clips reposted on social media, Hilton, appearing manic, could be seen in the livestream covered in blood, using an object to cut himself repeatedly. The Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office told Newsweek in a statement that deputies responded to Hilton’s home after the office received “multiple calls” about a person livestreaming acts of self-harm. After authorities confirmed Hilton was alone inside the home and spoke with family members at the scene, deputies decided to “tactically disengage while continuing to monitor the situation.” Related Stories Lifestyle Perez Hilton Claims He Encountered God After Being Hospitalized for Three Weeks Lifestyle Kate Moss, Joan Collins, Jerry Hall Set for 'Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie' Cameos “In many incidents involving a person experiencing a mental health crisis or actively harming themselves, deputies prioritize de-escalation by creating time, distance, and opportunities for communication,” the statement continued. “Unless there is an immediate threat to others, slowing the situation and utilizing crisis intervention techniques can reduce the likelihood of a suicide-by-cop encounter and minimize the risk of injury to the individual, deputies, and the public.” Local news station NBC6 , which had reporters at the scene, later reported that a man, believed to be Hilton, was seen being taken away in an ambulance. The sheriff’s office also confirmed to TMZ that “the individual has been safely recovered and transported by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue to a local hospital, where he is receiving medical attention.” The Hollywood Reporter has also reached out to the Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office for comment on the incident involving Hilton, in addition to his personal rep. Earlier this year, Hilton shared in a lengthy Instagram video that he was hospitalized for three weeks after initially battling the flu before developing “an ulcer, and then a perforation, and then Sepsis,” he said at the time. “The Sepsis just kept working and my body kept falling apart,” Hilton explained in the video in March. “Then one night with rapid response came ’cause my heart got out of control. They had to put me on heart medications. And then I developed another infection in the hospital.” He added, “It was just such a slow process. I mean, two weeks of just sickness and then another week of getting better before I was released. And that last week was hell because I had already been in the hospital two weeks by then. I was like, ‘I just wanna go home. I just want to be with my babies.’” Perez is a single father of three children. Once he was released from the hospital and sent back home, Hilton said he had time to reflect and came to the realization “that God presented Himself to me” during the challenging experience. “It was real and this has been life-changing. I’m so grateful,” he added at the time. “I’m excited to start taking the kids to church every week. And to just know that God is real. … I don’t have to hope to believe. I know now.” THR

Netflix ’s television adaptation of Fortune’s This Summer Will Be Different has found its main cast after receiving the greenlight in March of this year . The project continues in the current of success of Prime Video’s Every Year After , based on Fortune’s debut novel Every Summer After , which recently received a Season 2 renewal at Prime Video’s inaugural Obsessed Fest. Related Stories Books ‘Every Summer After’ Author Carley Fortune Details Involvement In Prime Video Adaptation: From Casting Sue To Future Of Her Literary Barry’s Bay Books 10 Major ‘Every Year After’ Book Changes From Carley Fortune’s Novel ‘Every Summer After’ For everything we know about the This Summer Will Be Different show heading to Netflix, read on. Watch on Deadline When will Netflix’s This Summer Will Be Different come out? There is no release date yet, as the show is in early stages of production. Has This Summer Will be Different started production yet? Yes, Netflix and author Carley Fortune revealed that the series has started production on Prince Edward Island, home of Anne of Green Gables . Who is in the cast of Netflix’s This Summer Will Be Different ? Deadline broke the news of the main trio’s casting, led by Sophie Nélisse ( Heated Rivalry , The Book Thief , Yellowjackets ) as Lucy Ashby. Next came the announcement of Roby Attal ( The Sex Lives of College Girls, The Haunting of Bly Manor )and Francesca Reale’s ( Stranger Things , Do Revenge ) casting as Clark siblings, Felix “Wolf” and Bridget . When Netflix unveiled the start of production, they also revealed that six actors had been added to round out the cast in recurring roles: Jordan Rodrigues as “Miles Lam,” Jude Wilson as “Zach”, Natalie Brown as “Christine”, James Tupper as “Ken”, Tom Barnett as “Peter” and Celia Owen as “Joy”. What is This Summer Will Be Different about? First published in 2024, Fortune’s third novel follows Lucy Ashby (Nélisse) as she drops everything at her florist job to come to the aid of her best friend Bridget (Reale), who gets cold feet about her upcoming wedding. The problem is, Lucy has a history with Bridget’s brother Felix (Attal) after a one night stand the night they met on PEI years ago. Bridget has three rules for Lucy’s trips to PEI, and the third is that Lucy not fall in love with Felix. Lucy and Bridget have been best friends since they began living together after college. Netflix’s logline calls the adaptation “a simmering, sun-soaked romance set across multiple summers on Prince Edward Island about Lucy, a young woman navigating her 20s and her first real love with her best friend’s brother, the one person she was never supposed to fall for.” Who else is behind Netflix’s This Summer Will Be Different ? Dane Clark ( Suze , One More Time ) and Linsey Stewart ( Workin’ Moms , North of North ) serve as creators and showrunners as well as executive producers. Author Carley Fortune will also executive produce alongside Jennifer Kawaja ( Sort Of, Wayward ), Elise Cousineau ( Cardinal , Small Achievable Goals ) and Sam Levine ( Small Achievable Goals , The Z Suite ) for Sphere Media. Directors are Karen Maine ( Yes, God, Yes , Nobody Wants This ), Jasmin Mozaffari ( Ginny & Georgia , Firecrackers ), Fab Filippo ( Sort Of , Save Me ). Does Carley Fortune have other book adaptations in development? Yes, Fortune’s One Golden Summer , which serves as a sequel of sorts to Every Summer After , will provide source material for Season 2 of Prime Video’s Every Year After . Her second novel, Meet Me At The Lake is in development with Netflix and Archewell Productions.

title: The Highest-Grossing Theater for ‘The Odyssey’ in 70MM Hadn’t Screened a New Movie in 35 Years
full_text: × Skip to main content By Gary Baum Plus Icon Gary Baum Senior Writer garymbaum Follow Sign Up View All August 4, 2026 4:03pm A 70mm screening of 'The Odyssey' at the Alex Theatre in Glendale, California. Photo by Erik Bakshi for Film Leader Co. Glendale’s century-old Alex Theatre installed its 70mm presentation system six weeks ago, just ahead of the July 17 premiere of The Odyssey . Now the venue, which hadn’t shown a first-run movie for 35 years, has announced it’s the highest grossing theatre in the country for Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic on the film format. “The response from audiences has been overwhelming and a wonderful reminder of how much people still value the shared experience of seeing a great film together,” Alex’s artistic director Miles Williams said in a statement which thanked Universal Pictures “for recognizing the important role historic theatres continue to play in Hollywood’s cinematic legacy.” The Odyssey ’s domestic box office total reached $395.5 million over the weekend. The film relinquished first place to Spider-Man: Brand New Day , Sony’s superhero sequel success story, which is sharing a portion of the Imax screens with Nolan’s movie. The 900-seat Alex, known for its mix of Classical Revival and Moderne architectural detailing, has been showing The Odyssey three times per day. The venue will be extending its run by at least two weeks. The marquee advertising The Odyssey at the Alex Theatre in Glendale, California. Photo by Erik Bakshi for Film Leader Co. Williams tells The Hollywood Reporter that the theatre — whose last first-run film was 1991’s Terminator 2: Judgment Day — is now scheduling eight to 10 nights of movie programming each month. (Its busy calendar is filled with live events, from ballet performances to rock concerts.) It intends to host periodic special engagements of other large-format releases, including Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three in December and Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew in February 2027. The Alex invested $500,000 in technical upgrades, including a new ground-floor projection booth. In-demand Los Angeles projectionist Taylor Umphenour, an Imax consultant who has worked with Nolan on his dailies, helped oversee the design and construction. “What you have at a cinema like the Alex is a true understanding of the in-person experience of shared narrative,” he says. “That’s why people are coming — and losing their minds.” A view from the open-air forecourt at the Alex Theatre. title: ‘Soulm8te’ Director Kate Dolan on Her Twisty Journey After ‘M3GAN 2.0’ and What That Ending Could Mean
full_text: Skip to main content David Rysdahl and Kate Dolan behind the scenes of 'Soulm8te.' Universal Pictures Home Entertainment Logo text [This story contains spoilers from Soulm8te .] Four years ago, Blumhouse struck gold with M3GAN , the story of a roboticist who creates an AI-powered doll to serve as a companion for her niece after the child loses her parents. The horror-comedy became a breakout hit with critics and audiences, grossing $180 million worldwide on a $12 million budget. However, last year’s M3GAN 2.0 failed to replicate that success. The sequel followed M3GAN being rebuilt to help combat a humanoid military robot, but it ultimately underperformed, grossing $39.1 million worldwide. Related Stories Movies 'Soulm8te' Review: Erotic Fembot Thriller From the M3GAN-Verse Is Enjoyably Lurid Pulp That Comes Up Short on Satirical Bite Movies 'Other Mommy' Trailer: Jessica Chastain Returns to Horror as a Body-Twisting Doppelganger That changed the trajectory for Soulm8te , a spinoff set in the M3GAN universe starring Lily Sullivan as Sara, an AI-powered companion for a grieving widower, David, played by David Rysdahl. But Sara quickly becomes dangerously obsessed. Kate Dolan’s feature was originally expected to follow in the franchise’s footsteps and debut in theaters. But the film was removed from Universal’s theatrical calendar in December, leaving its release plans uncertain. It was a surprise for Dolan and those involved, but last month, the world learned the film would make its way to audiences, with Blumhouse Atomic Monster announcing Soulm8te would premiere as a home entertainment release on Aug. 1. In a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter , Dolan, who co-wrote the screenplay with Rafael Jordan from a story credited to James Wan , Ingrid Bisu and Jordan, discusses crafting an erotic thriller spin on the AI doll, her future with Blumhouse Atomic Monster, why she is glad the film is reaching audiences at home, and comparisons to horror hit Obsession and the film’s ending. *** How did you balance the erotic thriller tone of this film without losing what audiences love about the M3GAN universe? That tone was the big question of how to balance those things. The reason James and Ingrid wanted to make this was because they love erotic thrillers and they wanted to make something that was true to that era of of filmmaking. And when I first spoke to James, he was referencing a lot of the classic erotic thriller films. And then they were like, OK but it needs to work in the M3GAN universe. So that was my biggest task initially — what’s the tone of this film, and how do we balance that? I watched a lot of films for reference, and films of that era are quite campy and can be — now looking back — quite fun in some ways. So I was just like mining what worked in those films and how to balance those tones together. James Wan is, of course, a horror maestro. What was it like collaborating with him so closely? For sure. It was something that he really wanted to do, so it was sort of his brainchild on doing this as a film. He’s such a wealth of knowledge in terms of filmmaking. He’s worked at the highest levels, and he obviously knows his genre really well. So it was always great to have him there as someone to bounce things off. And he would always look at set pieces, and he even came to set for a few days at one point when we had quite a heavy week of set pieces and stunts. It was great to have his input and insights because he obviously has done this many times before. This film reminded me of the 2013 film Her at times, and particularly, Lily’s voice as Sara, which sounded reminiscent of Scarlett Johansson’s performance. Was that movie a touchstone as you were working on this? Definitely. There were a lot of films that me and the cast watched when we were prepping the movie and the HODs as well. We watched a whole host of erotic thrillers and AI-related robot movies, as well as tonal references like [Paul] Verhoeven’s RoboCop. But Her was definitely one that we watched again. It was interesting watching Her how much has evolved since then, and what we can do to try and tell this story in the now. But even when I was starting to write the film, to when we were shooting, to now, how much things progress so quickly is really crazy. Stuff that we were writing that felt like science fiction months ago suddenly is happening, really, and it’s quite bizarre to experience. ( Laughs. ) But yeah, Her is a great movie. I think it was really ahead of its time in terms of what it was saying. It’s so interesting to watch it now, because it just feels so strange that that’s real. This film went through several changes before ultimately landing as a home entertainment release. Do you feel like Soulm8te was impacted by the reception to M3GAN 2.0? What explanation were you given for the change in release strategy? Yeah, I think M3GAN 2.0 was a big surprise for everybody, and it definitely impacted how Soulm8te was going to go out into the world. M3GAN 2.0 underperformed, and I think that was the main reason. The market is just so unpredictable these days. You don’t really know what’s going to happen or how something’s going to land. It can be very surprising sometimes. M3GAN in M3GAN 2.0. Universal Pictures How did you find out that it was going straight to home entertainment, and did you ever worry that audiences wouldn’t get to see the film? There was definitely a moment where I was concerned that we wouldn’t get to finish the film or people wouldn’t get to see it. So, I was really glad when I knew that it would be released at home because, as a filmmaker, when you’re doing your Dolby Atmos mix, you’re listening to big speakers. You’re hearing all the great sounds that you’re trying to do, and you want that, obviously, to be experienced in a theatrical space. But the bottom line is: What audiences buy into is story and character. That’s always been the case. That’s something that can be enjoyed in a theatrical space, or at home. A lot of movies I grew up loving, I watched at home, and I grew up watching on VHS, late night movies that would be on TV. I think it really allows the film to be seen by a really wide audience as well. A lot of people watch movies at home now, and that’s just part of our world and our culture. I’m just delighted that people are going to get to see the movie. And what a time we’re in for horror too — Original films like Obsession and Backrooms have exceeded expectations at the box office this year. When the trailer came out for Soulm8te, a lot of people were like, “This is like Obsession mixed with Companion .” Given that it explores similar themes, do you think it could have found an audience theatrically, post- Obsession success? You never know. It’s hard to [tell] — So, I’m not sure. But it’s funny the comparisons to Obsession because obviously this is a film that we made a while ago now, so it’s been a long time. And it’s funny seeing the comments, people being like, “Oh, this is just being Obsession. ” It’s like, “Well, we made this movie a long time ago.” ( Laughs .) But it’s so amazing to see those movies do well, and I’m such a fan of those films — I think [ Curry Barker and Kane Parsons] are great filmmakers. It’s very exciting. Anything that brings attention to horror and the genre, and a more mainstream audience into that niche, is like a rising tide lifts all boats. It’s a great time for original horror. If people find something in Soulm8te that’s like Obsession that makes them want to watch it, that’s great.​ In previous interviews, Jason Blum has been coy about whether M3GAN would appear in Soulm8te, which led to speculation. Now that we know she doesn’t appear, what was the thinking behind that decision? I think it was always going to be standalone — from the very first conversation I had about it. The team at Blumhouse Atomic Monster wanted this film to be its own thing and not have too much crossover with M3GAN. Also, tonally, the team there wanted to make something that felt a little darker, where they could push for the R rating, be a little more violent, or include sexual content. I felt it was better to do that as its own story, and we could push things a little more. Are there any Easter eggs from films in the franchise that audiences should keep an eye out for? Yeah, definitely. It was always going to be a standalone movie, but M3GAN 2.0 was actually prepping while I was writing the script for Soulm8te, and they were going into production close to when we were prepping. It was very abreast of each other, and I was always reading the latest drafts of M3GAN 2.0 and finding little things that I could put in that a fan of M3GAN could find in the movie, and they could link things. So yeah, there’s definitely stuff in there for sure. Can you tell me what in case myself or anyone else missed it at first? No, you gotta look out for them. They’re very subtle. But we also have a lot of references to different erotic thrillers. There’s the pub in the movie where they do the karaoke at the bar called the White Rabbit, and that was like a Fatal Attraction reference. There’s a lot of little small things in there that blink, and you miss them, but they’re there. David Rysdahl and Lily Sullivan in Soulm8te . Courtesy of Universal Pictures Home Entertainment There’s a particularly brutal death scene in the film. Why does Sara to use her sexuality as part of how she manipulates and kills her victims? That was always a reference back to the heyday of erotic thrillers in the ’80s and ’90s. I think the quote-unquote villain was always a very sexually promiscuous woman who was morally bankrupt, and she would often be using her feminine wiles to trick these men who were these innocent, quote-unquote, victims in this scenario. So, it was always riffing off that. But I always found the sex scenes in the movie, particularly with Sara, to be an abstract symbolism for how we interact with AI and how we’re lured in and we’re seduced in. It’s all symbolizing that — any scenes where she’s doing that are a manifestation of that idea. Early in the film, Sara says she can survive with water on her for up to 30 minutes. After she’s driven off the cliff, should audiences believe she could have survived? It was always set up that there’s a potential for that, because the thing with AI and tech is that no matter how much you delete something, it always exists in the digital ether and it survives in some way. You don’t know where those things can live on — and it’s something that we can’t comprehend. It’s not like you can destroy something anymore. There is always a risk that those things exist in the digital space, so it was just playing with that idea as well. I think, as humans, we see things in a very black-and-white way, but I think when it comes to that tech, it’s amorphous and we can’t really get control over it. So, there is a chance that she will survive and live on, and there’s not much we can do about that, really. At the end, we see another Soulm8te who looks like Sara but with dark hair introduced to David. Is that the real Sara? I mean, that’s up to the audience to decide if they want to believe it or not. The cast often asks me that, and I was like, “It’s up to you to decide if it is or not.” So, I’m not gonna say any more on that. ( Laughs. ) Do David and Aubrey (Claudia Doumit) end up together? Yeah, I was always rooting for them. I know we don’t see a conclusive result for them at the very end. But I feel like they have survived through this situation together, and they have a deep connection, which is clear. So, I’m always rooting for David and Aubrey. I think they make it in the end. Have James and Jason Blum talk to you about potentially directing another film for Blumhouse Atomic Monster after Soulm8te? We haven’t had that conversation yet. At the moment, I have some original ideas that I was writing over the past while. So I’m focused on working on those projects for now. But yeah, I’m always open to the idea of working with those guys again for sure. If Soulm8te is a hit on VOD, could you imagine doing more with it? I hadn’t thought about it too much, but recently there was this story about the New York school system thinking about having support teachers who were androids. I’d love a movie where Sara’s pretending to be human or pretending to be a teacher at a school, and we could do something fun with that to riff off that news story. But no, I haven’t thought about it too much. I mean, Lily is amazing as Sara, and I would love to see her in that role again. How have you navigated building your career as a female director in the horror genre? I can only speak to my own experience. I tend not to think of myself too much as a female [director]. Because then you start to think about the hurdles that you might face. I’ve always been working on projects that I love and feel connected to; putting as much into them as I possibly can. I’ve been very lucky in my career so far in that I’ve got to do some amazing things — but it’s tough. There’s a lot of unconscious bias in the industry, and there have been times when I’ve come up against that. There’s more you have to think about as a female filmmaker — how you come across on set and all of those kinds of things, which can be tricky. It’s sad to see some of the statistics of when those studies come out, and you see how few women are directing studio films, or films that are released theatrically. It’s definitely something that still needs to be talked about and looked at. But there’s so many amazing female filmmakers out there as well, who are making really cool films and doing amazing work. So, I always feel optimistic that the tables will turn and there will be more people getting to make movies. *** Soulm8te is now streaming digitally. THR

Shooting on the ten-part show will take place on Prince Edward Island and in Toronto, with Canadian producer Sphere Media attached. The creator-showrunners are Dane Clark ( Suze , One More Time ), and Linsey Stewart ( Workin’ Moms , North of North ). Logline on the series is as follows: “ This Summer Will Be Different , based on the beloved novel by Carley Fortune, is a simmering, sun-soaked romance set across multiple summers on Prince Edward Island about Lucy, a young woman navigating her 20s and her first real love with her best friend’s brother, the one person she was never supposed to fall for.” Related Stories Legal Producer Adds Defamation Claim To Lawsuit Against Netflix Over Theft Of Hard Drive Of World War II Espionage Pic 'Fortitude' News Idaho College Murders Doc Series Grabs Attention On Netflix; 'Ransom Canyon' Season 2 Off To Slow Start Exec producers are Clark, Stewart, Fortune and Jennifer Kawaja and Elise Cousineau for Sphere, the maker of Netflix limited series Wayward . Watch on Deadline “When Carley first entrusted us with her captivating book, we knew we had to find the right team to deliver to her passionate fanbase,” said Danielle Woodrow and Tara Woodbury, Netflix’s Directors, Content in Canada in a statement. “Developing this project with Dane, Linsey and Sphere has been a dream and we couldn’t have found better partners to bring this love letter to both Toronto and Prince Edward Island to the screen.” Fortune added: “I fell in love with Prince Edward Island first in the pages of L.M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables and again when I visited with my best friend in my early twenties. That vacation, the beauty of the island, the warmth of its people, and the friendships that sustain us – are the foundation of This Summer Will Be Different . I’m thrilled to bring this sweeping love story to the screen with Netflix and to transport audiences to the glittering shores and windswept beaches of PEI.” Netflix has been steadily upping its number of Canadian originals, which the streamer has linked to domestic viewing in Canada increasing 20% in 2025. full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie The Summer 50-Something Female Friendships Took Over Streaming With ‘Five Star Weekend’ & ‘Ride Or Die’s Surprise Success Disney Closes $1.2 Billion Deal To Sell A+E Global Media Stake To Hearst Viola Davis Stars In ‘Ascent’ Thriller Series Ordered By Paramount+ From John Logan View All March 16, 2026 1:45pm (L-R) Dana Walden and Debra OConnell Disney/ABC Dana Walden , incoming President and Chief Creative Officer of The Walt Disney Company as of Wednesday, has revealed the new leadership structure of Disney Entertainment. She laid out the changes Monday in a memo, which you can read below. In addition to television, which she oversaw; film, which she took over in her new role; and direct-to-consumer, which she co-ran with Disney’s film chief Alan Bergman , Walden’s purview now will include Games and Digital Entertainment, previously under incoming Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro, which will become part of Disney Entertainment, with Sean Shoptaw now reporting to Walden. Related Stories Executives Debra OConnell Sets Direct Reports, Including Craig Erwich Who Adds 20th Television Oversight Executives Disney Names Josh D’Amaro CEO, Dana Walden President & Chief Creative Officer Bergman and Shoptaw are members of Walden’s new leadership team of direct reports that also includes Debra OConnell , John Landgraf , Joe Earley and Adam Smith . Watch on Deadline There had been questions whether Bergman would stay on as Chairman of Disney Entertainment, Studios, under Walden. He will, as the two are said to be getting along great, and he also will continue to share oversight of Direct To Consumer (Disney+ and Hulu) with her. RELATE: Disney’s Josh D’Amaro On “Surreal” Moment He Was Asked To Be CEO; Incoming Chief Bonds With Dana Walden, Bob Iger At Town Hall With Walden expanding her turf as Disney President and CCO, there also had been a lot of speculation whether she would elevate one of her senior executives on the TV side to streamline the operation and reduce the number of her direct reports. She has, and that is OConnell, previously President, ABC News Group & Disney Entertainment Networks, who has been named to the newly created role of chairman of Disney Entertainment Television . OConnell now will be in charge of the television brands, including ABC Entertainment, Disney Branded Television, Hulu Originals, National Geographic Content and creative for 20th Television and 20th Television Animation, in addition to her current duties overseeing ABC News and the ABC Owned Television Stations. Her promotion only slightly impacts Landgraf, who remains Chairman of FX and will continue reporting directly to Walden and maintain oversight of Onyx Collective. He no will longer oversee Nat Geo, a brand that joined his portfolio in 2023. The network over the last couple of years pulled out of original scripted programming, Landgraf and his team’s top area of expertise. There will be a change for Eric Schrier , President of Disney Television Studios, who will report to Earley, having previously reported to Walden. DTC President Earley now will serve as Co-President of the division with Smith as both report to Walden. Earley heads content strategy for DTC, which explains Schrier’s alignment with him. Schrier serves as Head of Global Original Television Strategy, overseeing the development and production of international shows for Disney+, which is expected to be his priority going forward.
